item.title: Following the sudden closure of Bioware last night, people from across the games industry have shared their sympathies for those employees losing their jobs, and said farewell to one of the most influential RPG developers of all time. Read more
item.description:
Following the sudden closure of Bioware last night, people from across the games industry have shared their sympathies for those employees losing their jobs, and said farewell to one of the most influential RPG developers of all time.
The reactions come in many forms, with BioWare staff throughout the years looking back on their time at the studio and thanking their peers and fans for support. Game developers from other studios have paid tribute too, sharing their own tales of how Bioware impacted their careers.
"As much as it's not really a surprise," former Dragon age lead writer David Gaider on Bluesky, "especially given the industry right now coupled with the Saudi sale, the news today still made me sad ... BioWare joins other great studios of the past, with a legacy that will not soon be forgotten."
Former Knights of the Old Republic and Dragon Age lead James Ohlen also paid tribute to the studio, writing: "BioWare is closing. My 22 years there made me the man I am. The people affected today are some of the best RPG developers in the world. If you're hiring writers, designers, artists or engineers, start with them. Former BioWare folks: if an intro from me would help, reach out."
"This is sad news on multiple fronts," former Mass Effect boss and one-time BioWare general manager Casey Hudson added on X, "for those of us who worked there, for our friends and colleagues at BioWare who are impacted, and for fans who were looking forward to the next Mass Effect adventure.
"I started my career at BioWare and will forever be grateful to the founders, Greg and Ray, for inviting me to join in BioWare's legendary journey. Its legacy will live on through those who were part of it and continue to create games through a passion for unforgettable stories, worlds and characters."
"Remember BioWare is 100% owned by EA,” said Mark Darrah, former Dragon Age and Anthem executive producer in a YouTube video. “EA owns all the IPs. They own Dragon Age, they own Mass Effect, they own Jade Empire. That doesn’t change the situation, really, at all. [...] Now, there’s nobody working on a [BioWare] game, or games, within the EA organization, and chances are there never will be, which might make them more likely to sell off those IPs. But it might also make them more likely to just try to forget that they ever existed and bury them in the vault."
Trick Weekes, former narrative designer on the Mass Effect and Dragon Age series, posted a video from Mass Effect 3's Citadel DLC, in which Commander Shepard and their crew say a sombre farewell, while actor Mark Meer, the voice of male Shepard, shared his condolences and thanks with BioWare staff past and present.
Michael Gamble, who served as project director on the now-cancelled Mass Effect 5 until yesterday's layoffs also took to social media, thanking people for their support during his 17 years at the company, saying it "has meant everything to me."
While BioWare's closure prompted many studio alumni to share their thoughts, an outpouring of support and mourning came from outside the company too. "This is not something I ever expected to see," Swen Vincke, CEO of Baldur's Gate 3 developer Larian, wrote on social media. "Larian and Bioware started their trajectories in the games industry at the same time and Bioware led the way in making RPGs big. It's almost unimaginable that we're now entering an era where the name BioWare won't show up anymore when discussing upcoming RPGs. What a loss for all of us."
CD Projekt Red co-studio head Michał Nowakowski also recalled how important BioWare was to the Polish studio. "Bioware has been a massive part of CDPR history," he wrote. "We befriended them when localising and selling Baldur’s Gate games in Poland, Czech, and Slovakia. And later they were [a] great help when lending us their engine for Witcher 1, sharing their wisdom and even giving us a spot at their booth at E3. I had [the] pleasure to visit them a few times in Edmonton and also host them in our Warsaw office. Very sad for the people affected, but also sad to see a legendary brand go down. Not a great day in the games industry."
"Thank you for all the games. Thank you for the many hours of gameplay. Thank you for all the stories . You can be damned proud of what you achieved. I hope you all land well."
Nowakowski was joined by his peer Paweł Sasko, associate director of CD Projekt's upcoming Cyberpunk sequel, who revealed the importance of BioWare's games on his own career: "Baldur's Gate 1 and 2 shaped my imagination and the desire to create games. I would have never been here without BioWare igniting the fire in my heart. It inspired me, formed me, enriched my imagination, and for that I will be forever grateful. I will always remember you."
Dave Gilbert, founder of Old Skies and The Blackwell Legacy, similarly spoke of BioWare's impact on his career: "Eff me. Not Bioware, too. This one hurts more than most. I can't think of a studio that has had a bigger influence on me than this one. My dream was to be like them. I'll never stop feeling angry when studios with tremendous legacies just get bought and killed off for parts."
Some too had harsh words for EA and those behind Bioware's closure, alongside sympathy for those affected. Legendary immersive sim developer Warren Spector, for instance, decried the fact the development team had now been left "out in the cold with so many others."
"BioWare is more than just another studio," he continued. "For decades it’s played a central role in the history of our medium. They, for many years, as effectively as any studio, married art and commerce. Their work changed things. This is such bad news, such a devastating historic event all I can say is that it’s utter bullshit. Anyone who participated in this travesty should be ashamed.
"Actually, maybe all of the people who participated — the folks in suits (real or virtual) should lose their damn jobs. I ask them to ponder this: What do you contribute to gaming? What price do you pay for failure? I’d love to see THEM on the unemployment line instead of the people who do real work. Why is it always the do-ers and makers who pay the price? Someone explain that to me!"
Following news of BioWare's closure, EA confirmed other sweeping changes across the company, which will result in a total of 400 job cuts. While it did not explicitly name the other studios impacted by the move, employees have already started posting on social media, revealing the likes of Respawn, Maxis, Full Circle, EA Motive, and Ripple Effect have all been impacted. The layoffs come after EA was fully acquired by a consortium made up of Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, investment firm Silver Lake, and private equity company Affinity Partners for $55bn earlier this year.
Eurogamer wishes all those impacted by the layoffs the very best for the future.

item.title: EA announced overnight it's closing Mass Effect and Dragon Age studio BioWare in a new round of cuts that include the elimination of 400 roles across the publisher. But while it confirmed BioWare's 50 workers are affected, and that Skate studio Ripple Effect was being downsized, it did not say where the other 350 job cuts would come from. Read more
item.description:
EA announced overnight it's closing Mass Effect and Dragon Age studio BioWare in a new round of cuts that include the elimination of 400 roles across the publisher. But while it confirmed BioWare's 50 workers are affected, and that Skate studio Ripple Effect was being downsized, it did not say where the other 350 job cuts would come from.
Now, however, new information has emerged revealing The Sims studio Maxis, Battlefield support studio Ripple Effect, and EA Motive are all impacted by layoffs, alongside Full Circle and BioWare. That's according to Vertical Slice, citing an "anonymous source" supported by corroborating information on LinkedIn.
Maxis senior director Anna Huerta and three Ripple Effect artists - Brandon Garcia, Corey Thomas, and Turner Spring - confirmed their departure from EA on LinkedIn. Catheryn Grant, operations product manager at both Ripple Effect and Respawn, also revealed she was among those impacted, as was EA Motive's senior gameplay designer Jamieson Shearer. Full Circle's senior designer David Milne and seasonal creative director John Epler are affected too.
In a memo to staff shared overnight, EA said it had paused development of an unannounced Sims project called Project Lotus in order to focus on a different title dubbed Project Evergreen. The company also said it was downsizing Full Circle to "create an experience that keeps [players] engaged over the long-term", so there was already some suggestion those studios would face job cuts.
More surprising, though, are the cuts at Respawn, a studio EA said it would be investing "heavily" in to support the growth of free-to-play shooter Apex Legends. Respawn is also co-developing a new project alongside DICE, which is reportedly Star Wars: Battlefront 3. By the same token, EA said it's throwing its "full weight behind" Motive Studio's Iron Man game and Respawn's Star Wars Jedi sequel, its only two action-adventure projects currently in the works.
This is the first round of layoffs at EA since the company was fully acquired by a consortium made up of Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, investment firm Silver Lake, and private equity company Affinity Partners earlier this year. The trio acquired EA in the summer for $55bn in one of the largest leveraged buyout deals ever.
When the deal closed, EA told debt investors it would cut $700m in annual costs, including $170m in "organisational efficiencies". At the time, many feared that would translate to major layoffs.

item.title: Microsoft has revealed how much its Xbox cloud gaming service is going to cost, with 50 hours of stream-time selling for an introductory price of $11.99. Read more
item.description:
Microsoft has revealed how much its Xbox cloud gaming service is going to cost, with 50 hours of stream-time selling for an introductory price of $11.99.
This information comes from a post on the official Xbox news website, which explains that starting today, Xbox Insiders will be able to stream games using the paid service without needing an active Game Pass subscription. This comes ahead of a planned rollout to all Xbox players in November. These paid packs provide an ad-free version of the free cloud gaming service revealed earlier this year.

It's worth noting that even people paying for the Xbox cloud streaming service will encounter wait times during peak hours, though the blog post stated these waits will be shorter.
Microsoft previously revealed that monthly time limits will be placed on its paid Xbox cloud gaming service, though it insisted only a fraction of players would run into this cut-off point. A report claimed a 15-hour cap placed on the Game Pass Ultimate cloud gaming service was present as that's the moment Xbox starts losing money. Offering a cloud gaming service requires server infrastructure, compute costs, and network and bandwidth costs.
As an aside, Sony's defunct cloud gaming service PlayStation Now used to charge $9.99 for a month of streamed game time, more than a decade ago.
Xbox is currently in the midst of a massive restructuring process, in which more than 3,000 employees are to be laid off from the company. In a recent report, additional waves of layoffs are said to be planned for later this month, November, and January.

item.title: A new Star Wars: Battlefront game is reportedly in the works, and it's said to have Apex Legends and Star Wars Jedi studio Respawn working on it, as well as Battlefield and Battlefront developer DICE. Read more
item.description:
A new Star Wars: Battlefront game is reportedly in the works, and it's said to have Apex Legends and Star Wars Jedi studio Respawn working on it, as well as Battlefield and Battlefront developer DICE.
The information comes from "multiple sources" on Variety, and arrives in the wake of EA's sudden decision to lay off 400 workers, close iconic role-playing game studio BioWare, and cancel several projects. As part of a memo to staff, EA executives confirmed that Respawn and DICE are collaborating on a new project, but stopped short of saying what it was.
The report follows days of murmurings from different sources that a third Battlefront game is in the works. It started with a rumour from Electronic Gaming Monthly magazine (via Giant Bomb), which said Disney had been on the lookout for a studio to develop Battlefront 3. The names of potential teams included DICE, and Destiny and Marathon developer Bungie.
Wardogs studio head Joe Brammer then responded to the rumour on X, saying it was actually DICE and Respawn working together on Battlefront 3 - information that now appears to be true.
In 2022, EA was said to have cancelled multiple Star Wars projects in development at the time, including a follow-up to Battlefront 2. That most recent game in the Battlefront series launched in 2017 to a mixed reception. The launch version is mostly remembered for introducing loot boxes to the series that assigned random chance to earning functional in-game characters and powers. It was universally disliked. The backlash was so disastrous it kicked off a wave of legislation worldwide that deemed loot boxes to be gambling mechanics, the fallout of which persists to this day.
DICE would end up overhauling many of those systems and removing loot boxes altogether. The developer turned Battlefront 2's fortunes and player sentiment around, continuing to support the game for years, before releasing its final major update in 2020.
Battlefront 3 would be the first in the series to be published by the now Saudi-owned EA. Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, together with investment firm Silver Lake and private equity company Affinity Partners, acquired EA in the summer for $55bn in a leveraged buyout deal.

item.title: Not only is EA closing down BioWare and cancelling the next Mass Effect - Electronic Arts has now announced a heap of drastic changes that include cutting 400 jobs across the company, pausing development on a project connected to The Sims, and bringing together Respawn and DICE. Read more
item.description:
Not only is EA closing down BioWare and cancelling the next Mass Effect - Electronic Arts has now announced a heap of drastic changes that include cutting 400 jobs across the company, pausing development on a project connected to The Sims, and bringing together Respawn and DICE.
In a memo first sent to staff and later published online, CEO David Tinson and CSO Cam Weber first took a moment to thank employees before letting them know they might lose their jobs.
"Today, we're the number one publisher in Western HD gaming," the duo wrote. "That's an extraordinary position to lead from, and one we should be proud of. Yet our industry is changing quickly. Players have more choices than ever for their time and attention, competition is intensifying, and some of our biggest opportunities for growth are beyond the markets, platforms, and business models where EA has traditionally been the strongest."
The executives then laid out some changes to its portfolio of games. Top of the list is the closure of BioWare, the legendary role-playing powerhouse behind games such as Mass Effect and Dragon Age. Bloomberg reports around 400 jobs will be cut as part of the cost-cutting changes, including roughly 50 job cuts at BioWare.
As for The Sims, the publisher claims it's prioritising something called "Project Evergreen" and is giving "the team more time to reach the full potential and vision for the game." To do so, the execs said they're "pausing development" on another Sims-related title called "Project Lotus." The early access Skate reboot (skate.) has apparently "had a lot of success," but the publisher is still restructuring the studio into a "more focused, smaller team," regardless.
Marvel's Iron Man game (the one that leaked recently) and a third Star Wars Jedi game remain untouched, apparently, though it sounds like we'll see fewer big-budget action-adventure games come from the publisher going forward: "Beyond that, we will concentrate our efforts on fewer simultaneous, large-scale projects, ensuring that every game we build in this space is fully set up for success."
EA also re-emphasised its commitment to Apex Legends and the Battlefield series after the success of Battlefield 6. But that's not all. "We'll be bringing together our Respawn and DICE studios to collaborate on a future project." There's been some rumblings about a possible Star Wars: Battlefront follow-up this week, though EA doesn't give any more concrete details about what this game could be.
Then there's the publisher's golden goose, EA Sports. The executives said they're still committed to FC and the rest of its sport simulations, alongside two new projects that'll be revealed in the next few months - the return of Fight Night and a "brand-new, social-first open-world experience for our American Football team that we call 'Project Gridiron'".
"The decisions we’re making in our priorities, how we work, and with our portfolio reflect our belief in EA’s future. Some open exciting new possibilities. Others are difficult, especially for the people and teams across the company who are directly affected. In those cases, we will support impacted employees in exploring other opportunities within EA, and we're committed to treating impacted colleagues with care and respect," the executives added.
A group of investment firms led by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund took EA private earlier this summer, in a deal worth around $55 billion.

item.title: After over three decades of iconic RPGs, developer BioWare is closing down and its in-development Mass Effect game is no more. The move comes just months after corporate owner EA was bought out by a group of investment firms for $55 billion. Read more
item.description:
After over three decades of iconic RPGs, developer BioWare is closing down and its in-development Mass Effect game is no more. The move comes just months after corporate owner EA was bought out by a group of investment firms for $55 billion.
"For more than 30 years, BioWare has been more than a studio. It has been a home for storytellers, developers, and the players who brought our worlds to life," the role-playing powerhouse wrote on social media this evening before listing some of its greatest hits - Baldur's Gate, Neverwinter Nights, Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic, Dragon Age, Mass Effect and Anthem.
"Now, after more than three decades of shared adventures, BioWare is closing and early development on the next Mass Effect project is ending. There is nothing easy about writing those words. Our focus right now is on our incredibly talented team who put their hearts into these games, and supporting one another through this transition."
"What generations of BioWare built together is something to celebrate and remember. These games became so much more because you played them, debated your choices, fell in love with the characters, and made these worlds your own. From all of us at BioWare, thank you for being the most meaningful part of our story," the statement continued.
Layoffs at BioWare were expected following EA's acquisition this summer - which saw investment firm Silver Lake, private equity group Affinity Partners (led by Jared Kushner, Donald Trump's son-in-law) and Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund group together and raise $55 billion to buy the publisher. A full studio closure this soon is a surprise, to put it lightly.
A Bloomberg report also claims EA is planning to cut roughly 400 jobs across the company, or around 3 percent of its total workforce. "Across our portfolio, we're making deliberate choices to align talent and investments where we see the greatest opportunities for players and long-term growth," CEO David Tinson and CSO Cam Weber said in a letter to staff seen by Bloomberg.
BioWare itself has been in rough waters these past few years. The studio's live-service experiment Anthem quickly fell from the sky, and its most recent game, Dragon Age: The Veilguard, failed to meet EA's internal sales expectations, leading to another round of layoffs at the developer. Here's hoping the impacted devs can land on their feet soon.
The next Mass Effect game - dubbed Mass Effect 5 by some fans - was seemingly not ready to go into full production. Last we heard, BioWare was trying to reassure folks the game was still definitely in development.

item.title: Developer One More Level is wall-running toward another big success with its recently-released first-person Soulslike, Valor Mortis, which has already broken even after its first week. Read more
item.description:
Developer One More Level is wall-running toward another big success with its recently-released first-person Soulslike, Valor Mortis, which has already broken even after its first week.
The studio best known for shoot-and-slash series Ghostrunner celebrated the milestone earlier today. "We are beyond proud to announce that Valor Mortis has officially reached a break-even point in just seven days," the developer wrote in a recent social media post.
"This incredible milestone wouldn't be possible with you," it added. "Thank you for answering the Emperor's call and believing in our vision!"
We are beyond proud to announce that @ValorMortis has officially reached a break-even point in just 7 DAYS! This incredible milestone wouldn't be possible without YOU. Thank you for answering the Emperor's call and believing in our vision! https://t.co/w0Bh6y2YrO
Breaking even means Valor Mortis has officially made back the money that was spent on its production - every sale from here on out is presumably pure profit for One More Level and the game's publisher, Lyrical Games.
What makes the achievement even more impressive is that Valor Mortis came out in perhaps the most hectic period for new games we've seen in years. The inevitable black hole known as GTA 6 understandably crammed tons of games into the months before and after its November release date - heavy hitters such as Control Resonant, Onimusha: Way of the Sword, Silent Hill Townfall, Gears of War: E-Day, Marvel's Wolverine, and many more launched mere weeks or sometimes even days apart from each other. (Take a look at our upcoming games calendar and you'll see what I mean.)
Still, the historical first-person action game managed to grapple to success largely thanks to a warm reception. Eurogamer's Valor Mortis review praised the ways in which it went above and beyond the typical Soulslike formula. Here's what our Matt Wales had to say: "Valor Mortis is a delight; a gloriously entertaining Soulslike whose fluid foundational combat and cleverly designed enemy encounters would probably be enough on their own. But then One More Level goes further: the exhilarating parkour, the thrilling sense of momentum that shapes everything from the intricate level design and memorable bosses to the sword- and gunplay, elevating it further."
One More Level was also pretty open about releasing a game during such a chaotic time. The developer previously explained that Valor Mortis costs £40/$40 because it knew "this fall is stacked and there's high demand for your time and money." The studio smartly pushed the game out of its original 24th September release date, too, which would've had it going toe-to-to with both Control Resonant and Silent Hill Townfall.
Valor Mortis launched last week across PC, PS5, Xbox Series X/S and Game Pass. When asked about DLC and future patches, the dev simply replied "Working on it!"

item.title: CD Projekt Red has detailed the substantial update coming to Cyberpunk 2077, revealing a new dual-wielding skill for pistols and revolvers, cyberware customisation, cross-platform mod support, and a brand-new Edgerunners-related story quest featuring voice actors from the Netflix anime show. Read more
item.description:
CD Projekt Red has detailed the substantial update coming to Cyberpunk 2077, revealing a new dual-wielding skill for pistols and revolvers, cyberware customisation, cross-platform mod support, and a brand-new Edgerunners-related story quest featuring voice actors from the Netflix anime show.
The update arrives 22nd October on PC, PS5, and Xbox Series S/X, with the Switch 2 version following "in a couple of days", CDPR media manager Laura Beitzel said during a RedStream this afternoon.
Actual details on the new Edgerunners-related story quest were intentionally thin, but Cyberpunk 2 associate game director Pawel Sasko said it had been written with people involved in the Netflix show, and CDPR publishing producer Natlia Pych it would be a prequel to Edgerunners 2. "It will be the last job of the King's team," Pych said, and it will let us meet characters on the team: Emily, Meshuga, and Miguel.
There'll also be a new Edgerunners radio station added to Cyberpunk 2077 to listen to, which has 16 tracks comprised of songs from both Edgerunners 1 and 2, Sasko said.
Another new type of quest coming in the update is Night City Tours, which is a less action-focused pursuit - the word "cosy" was thrown around. Night City founder Richard Night tells you the lore of the city while things happen around him that don't quite seem to add up. This is a mystery you need to solve. There are also minor tarot arcana being added to the game for you to find, in conjunction with an actual physical deck going on sale.
Cross-platform mod support in Cyberpunk 2077 comes hot on the heels of cross-platform mod support being added to the Remastered update for The Witcher 3, and it works in a very similar way. It's also a partnership with mod platform Mod.io, and there's a panel in the game where you can browse mods - "including the adult mods", Sasko said with a smile - and download and install them. And this is a work in progress: more mods will be added over time.
Implantable cyberware is becoming customisable via new "glam docs" being added to the game alongside - sometimes literally - the ripper docs you already find there. There are five new glam docs dotted around the city, each with their own shop space, and each offering bespoke visual upgrades. This allows you to colour your implants the way you want them.
Beside that, there are a "ton" of new optimisations coming to the game, including a field of vision slider at long last, proper DLSS 4.5 support, and metal frame interpolation and denoising on Mac, whatever that is - it sounded like it was a big deal.

item.title: Beyond Good & Evil 2 is reportedly still in pre-production a staggering 18 years after it was first announced, and it has apparently evolved from being a multiplayer-first project to being "solo-first" and story based, with additional, optional co-op. Read more
item.description:
Beyond Good & Evil 2 is reportedly still in pre-production a staggering 18 years after it was first announced, and it has apparently evolved from being a multiplayer-first project to being "solo-first" and story based, with additional, optional co-op.
Origami Media (in a French report translated by DeepL) said it heard from several people close to the game's development that the idea for Beyond Good and Evil 2, in 2019-2022, was for the game to be "highly multiplayer and connected", featuring "a multitude of planets" where players would be matchmade and play together. Sound familiar? It's supposed to.
"The key concept was the 'third place' - a spot where you might hang out with mates after work, just as you would in Fortnite or Destiny," Origami shared, "which were cited as sources of inspiration. You played as a blank character, tagging along on the adventures of the heroes of Beyond Good & Evil, in the passenger seat."
But since then, the project "evolved", from smaller matchmade groups to more open-ended play, then to team-based play in groups of four and finally, to pairs. "The aim now is to offer a 'solo-first' adventure, with no mandatory online connection and featuring a strong narrative that can also be played in co-op," Origami stated.
"A few years ago, some people thought it bore a resemblance to Zelda in space; today, its combat is very reminiscent of Insomniac's Spider-Man games."
Yet despite its incredible length of time in development - I was at the Paris-based UbiDays event in 2008 when Ubisoft revealed the first CGI trailer for Beyond Good and Evil 2 - the game is apparently yet to enter full production. "If we go by the terminology used at Ubisoft and in many other major companies in the sector," Origami went on, "production of BGE2 has not yet begun. It is currently in pre-production, which still involves at least 250 people (at Ubisoft Montpellier alone). And this project is now aiming to move into the alpha phase."
According to the report, "Historically, BGE2 has failed to meet all its creative milestones." These are referred to as "gates", which sound like playable builds of the game, and it kept missing these because ideas about the game kept changing. "Is the game cool enough? Innovative? Can we make this loop more engaging? Hang on, let's push the deadline back again - we could improve the combat system... and so on," Origami wrote.
The reason the unfinished game survived so long was because it had "unwavering" support from Ubisoft. "It was impossible for it to be cancelled," Origami added. "To the point where it became something of a poison, according to several people within the company. If the project is never cancelled, could it also never be finished?"
But wide-ranging restructuring at Ubisoft, which most recently caused the closure of Trials developer RedLynx and the downsizing of the Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced team in Ubisoft Singapore - and reportedly layoffs at Germany offices too - has pulled that rug of invincibility from under the project. "They are now being told, rather more matter-of-factly: 'We don't know what's going to happen.'" One source said this was a "return to a sense of reality".
Beyond Good and Evil 2 holds the record for the video game longest in development, having surpassed Duke Nukem Forever's 14-year record in 2022. The game came closest to being realised, seemingly, in around 2018, when Ubisoft showed Beyond Good and Evil 2 to press - including Eurogamer - behind closed doors at E3, and promised a playable beta towards the end of 2019. But that never materialised. More recently, the game got a new creative director, and job adverts for the project have been sporadically appearing, including one spotted the other day.

item.title: World of Warcraft: Forever's beta has been extended until this Friday, much to the joy of the community of early players. Read more
item.description:
World of Warcraft: Forever's beta has been extended until this Friday, much to the joy of the community of early players.
Announced on X by World of Warcraft's Associate production director Clayton Stone, this extension will allow those who have hopped into the MMO for their level 1-30 journey to spend just a little bit more time before servers go down this weekend.
In addition Blizzard is hosting a server stress test today, allowing players - including those who otherwise wouldn't have access to the beta - a chance to hop on and bush the game to its limits. After the servers go down on Friday, WoW Forever lovers will have a chance to reserve a character name next week, ahead of the full launch on the 4th November.
This obviously is great news for those who can't get enough of World of Warcraft: Forever, but there's a funny consequence to this extension. On World of Warcraft community hubs, players made lovely farewell posts to the game ahead of the original beta end date. Like this one, where Reddit user Roodster123 sat their gnome down overlooking the Stormwind docks in a post titled "This is where I leave you little one. We had a good run. Until we meet again."
While it's maybe a little late to hop on now, World of Warcraft: Forever's beta gave an excellent first impression to the upcoming MMO. That obviously is brilliant for those excited to dive back into Azeroth, and equally tragic for those of us unable to get time off work.

item.title: AMD, the company that designs the chips inside Xbox and PlayStation consoles, made a big announcement this week: it's bringing the latest version of its advanced, AI-driven image upscaling technology, FSR 4.1, to Xbox Series X, Series S, and handhelds ROG Ally and Ally X. Read more
item.description:
AMD, the company that designs the chips inside Xbox and PlayStation consoles, made a big announcement this week: it's bringing the latest version of its advanced, AI-driven image upscaling technology, FSR 4.1, to Xbox Series X, Series S, and handhelds ROG Ally and Ally X.
An older version of FSR is already supported on Xbox, but FSR 4.1 is its most advanced release. You may recall FSR 4.1 arrived on Steam Machine and Steam Deck shortly after the former's launch in the summer, and it has proven to be a useful option for players looking for a sharper image.
FSR works by rendering the game at a lower resolution, which is then upscaled to a higher resolution by using machine learning algorithms. This allows supported hardware to deliver better quality visuals without putting extra strain on hardware, or by giving more consistent performance.
While all Xbox platforms stand to benefit from FSR 4.1's arrival, Series S and the more hardware-constrained Ally and Ally X handhelds could see the biggest gains. In that way, Microsoft is extending the life of the Series consoles by allowing its aging hardware to do more.
The timing of this announcement is particularly notable, too, as just a couple of weeks ago, Sony introduced QSSR - a similar machine learning-based upscaling technology - for PlayStation 5. QSSR is the less capable sibling of PSSR, which is exclusive to PS5 Pro.
FSR 4.1's arrival also comes as new reports suggest Xbox's next generation Project Helix consoles could cost upwards of $1,800, which would significantly hinder its adoption rate, considering its price.
"We've worked very closely with AMD to optimise this technology, giving developers another powerful tool for great performance and visual quality for players," said Xbox chief technology officer (CTO) Scott Van Vliet.
"And this is just the beginning. Our teams are continuing to work together across hardware and software, and there's even more ahead with Project Helix, leveraging FSR Diamond to power what comes next."
AMD did not offer a specific date as to when FSR 4.1 will arrive on Xbox Series consoles, but it's going to be interesting to see how the image quality compares to PS5's QSSR.

item.title: Who doesn't love a big swing, a bold new direction, especially when so many video game publishers seem increasingly determined to walk the safest route? While Stranger Than Heaven might look familiar at first glance - particularly if you're a fan of Like a Dragon developer RGG's other third-person action games - it differs where it counts. item.description:
Who doesn't love a big swing, a bold new direction, especially when so many video game publishers seem increasingly determined to walk the safest route? While Stranger Than Heaven might look familiar at first glance - particularly if you're a fan of Like a Dragon developer RGG's other third-person action games - it differs where it counts. And to my mind, it's one of the most exciting games the studio has worked on in a while.
Stranger Than Heaven tells the story of Makoto Daito, a man of half American and Japanese lineage, as he attempts to make a home for himself in Japan. It's a tale spanning numerous decades as the country evolves - decades you'll experience first-hand as the story unfolds - blending a strong narrative throughline with striking melee combat and touches of silliness too. Its Like a Dragon heritage is clear, but it also feels like so much more.
Three things in particular stood out after a few hours of play: Stranger than Heaven's brilliant approach to fighting, the setting's gradual evolution through the years, and the surprisingly musical heart of it all.
Now, the combat, I suspect, will be divisive. Rather than replicating Like a Dragon's trusty action, Stranger than Heaven assigns your left and right strikes to your controller's triggers and bumpers. Attacks are hefty and weightier than other RGG games, the shift in set-up making each blow reverberate through the gamepad.
There's also a strong emphasis on parrying and dodging, encouraging players to spot the direction of an incoming attack and respond with a manual defensive manoeuvre matching that direction. An enemy throwing a haymaker from the right can be deflected with a well-timed right parry, for instance, and a goon slicing at your portside from off screen? Dodging back enables you to weave under the attack.
Stranger than Heaven is also one of the most explicitly violent action games RGG has produced, save perhaps for Like A Dragon's zombie-themed spin-off Dead Souls or Like a Dragon: Ishin. Here, Daito slits throats, stabs, bludgeons, and otherwise evercerates people in regular combat. There's also a takedown mechanic that, with the simultaneous press of two triggers, allows you to eliminate enemies on low health using some particularly brutal finishers.
While it took me a few minutes to get used to the control scheme, I quickly grew to adore it. Something about the more purposeful controls, combined with excellent animation work, made the fights feel ferocious and ripped straight from the best action flicks. It's the sort of combat that makes your body shift left and right alongside your character. At the same time, though, it's different enough that it requires work to master, particularly the crucial parry timing, and I fear many will run against it like a wall rather than endure the climb to greater heights of enjoyment. The game felt at its best when I was vigorously throwing myself into brawls, and I fear some may feel encouraged to approach fights purely reactively.
When you throw yourself into a fight, slinging punches and grappling enemies to the ground, the game takes an almost savage turn. Brawls are often dirty, explosive bouts. You get pounded with a heavy punch, dodge the next hit, and tackle them to the ground. Tenderize them with a few punches of your own, then finish 'em off with a grisly slam of their head against the hard ground. When you rise, you'll see other enemies stumble back in fear. Leap into Stranger than Heaven, and the fights reach bloody-raw peaks that'll stick in your mind.
As for Stranger Than Heaven's setting, it's truly wonderful, taking you from the smoke-choked skyline of 1915 Kokura, to a bustling 1929 Kure, a buzzing 1943 Minami, and beyond. Hopping between each era in turn (I encountered them in linear fashion, and that appears to be the case in the full game), I was struck by the world-building. RGG has always been great at depicting the modern era, and has successfully recreated the past too, but I was thoroughly impressed by what feels like a particularly soulful depiction of a gradually changing Japan.
As I walk the dark and dreary streets of Kure, people-watching in this burgeoning city, the detail is striking. Kure's inhabitants sit around drinking and eating, they roam its abodes and alcoves, chatting with others they meet. And the 1930s-adjacent period flourishes - the theatrical posters and the rumble of early automobiles trundling through the streets - all of it is wonderful.
If Kure made me pause, 40s-era Minami knocked me on my arse. The way its entertainment district clashes against old wooden docks creates a brilliant contrast, as rundown houses sit below bougie new buildings, encapsulating the wave of modernisation sweeping Japan. There's something mesmerising about the world changing as your character does too. In Kokura, at the start of the game, Daito is a struggling, dirty brawler looking to make a home in an often hostile country. By 1943, he's a reflection of the lively world around him. I left wanting to see more.
Then, of course, there's the music. Stranger Than Heaven's main management minigame sees players running a musical revue, Daito picking songs and stage accompaniments for performances throughout the decades. Only a few days ago, Sega released an Act One story trailer in which he sings a little song for the people of Kokura, and it's safe to say that music matters in Stranger than Heaven.
I only had time to organise one show during my hands-on, but I was able to pick different singers and musicians, as well as alter each song's mood. You can compose new variations of unlocked music, switching a lively track to a sombre one for example, which may better suit an upcoming show. How it'll all come together, I don't yet know , but given the many wonderful evenings I've sunk into karaoke in previous RGG games, I'm down for this more extravagant, elaborate twist. Snoop Dogg, I should add, did not perform a song in-game, though he did teach me how to roll cigarettes and the joys of blending different herbs.
Stranger than Heaven stuck in my teeth like taffy, and I was still tasting its sweetest bits for a while after playing. All this from an appetiser: if the full game manages to maintain the level of quality I saw throughout the entire game then I reckon this younger generation of RGG generation has a bright future ahead of them.

item.description:
Infinity Ward opened up early access to Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4's DMZ extraction mode overnight, meaning anyone who has pre-ordered a copy can now play the game's campaign as well as DMZ. And while early reactions to DMZ are fairly positive, there's one issue in particular, which a number of players have experienced, that has the capability of ending a round as soon as it begins.
The issue is to do with where DMZ spawns players. As an extraction shooter, DMZ's Hajin map offers multiple random spawn locations, and unlike traditional multiplayer modes, DMZ spawns are often on the edges of the map - far away enough from any action to allow players a chance to strategise and pick a target destination.
But unfortunately, one of the spawn-points Infinity Ward picked happens to be placed in the middle of a road, meaning that if you're unlucky, you might spawn as an enemy patrol is driving on it, flattening you and ending your round.
This nearly happened to Reddit user grillimperator, who was given a small window of time to jump out of the way. Reddit user Deep-Operation-3552, however, wasn't so lucky, immediately falling to the ground as soon as they got control of their character after the infil cutscene. As others noted in the replies, the timing of the 'Welcome to the DMZ' voice alert playing just as they die makes it all the more absurd. Judging by those examples, at least, there doesn't appear to be any form of spawn protection.
DMZ offers certain options to get back up after being downed, but if you don't have the necessary equipment, there's nothing you can do. Still, that wouldn't have mattered in the above instances, because the players were run over twice.
Given the persistent nature of DMZ, dying also means losing everything you entered the match with, which could be infuriating if that was the round you decided to pack your good gear.
Thankfully, the bug is one of several issues Infinity Ward fixed in a new DMZ patch. The patch notes specifically called out the problem: "Fixed some instances where enemy AI could run over players while infilling."
Modern Warfare 4's final mode, traditional multiplayer, unlocks at the game's full launch this Friday, 23rd October on PC, PS5, Xbox Series X/S and Switch 2. So far, players appear to be happy with the game's campaign, making it of the most well-received COD games on Steam. One player even managed to finish the campaign on its hardest, single-life mode YOLO.

item.description:
Right, let's get one important thing out of the way first: I've played a fair bit more of Dawn of War 4's main campaign, after my initial impressions of a single mission last year, and I think it is very good. The action is as screen-filling as ever, the Orks are a delight, and the combat director, which sees individual combatants lock onto each other with bespoke animations when groups fight in melee, remains a genuine feat of RTS engineering. I'll have much more to say on that front soon, though I'd like a little more time with it first.
And so, in the meantime, I bring huge* news.
(*This is not likely to be huge news to very many people at all.)
That news is, amongst other things, confirmation of how and why developer King Art decided on the colour of the Blood Ravens' chestplate "imperialis". For the un-neckbearded out there, this is a big deal amongst a very specific part of the 40K community. Warhammer is, ultimately, a tabletop game and hobby built around painting miniatures, and given the nature of it - and of its audience, really, myself included - that painting process has developed all kinds of rules, which are in turn governed by the series' ludicrously vast repository of lore.
The good news is the Warhammer community is also surprisingly good at enforcing the "rule of cool" when it comes to painting minis - as in, if you think it looks cool, then you go for it and don't let anybody stop you. But there are also plenty who want to know exactly what the lore says about the exact piece of armour you're about to paint. And to those people who happen to also be Blood Ravens fans, that's led to the question of the imperialis - the winged skull marking on Space Marine chestplates - and what colour it's truly meant to be.
This is because, in the original Dawn of War games, that imperialis was gold. But then in Dawn of War 2 and 3, it changed to black. In the meantime, Games Workshop, the company behind the 40K universe, has offered very little in terms of wider lore for the Blood Ravens chapter of the Space Marines. Unlike others such as the poster-boy Ultramarines, they have no origin story or confirmed "gene seed" - essentially their genetic origins, a huge part of 40K lore - and likewise varying depictions in official imagery. Even Games Workshop itself has varied over the years, with an old White Dwarf magazine's depiction being one of the main sources until a recent official in-house recipe was confirmed by one persistent fan. (In that version, it was plain old black - boo!)
Amongst all this, and particularly with the original games in mind, I was curious as to what the conversations between King Art's Dawn of War team and Games Workshop looked like when it came to settling on the armour scheme for Dawn of War 4, which has opted for black again here. It turns out, as game director Jan Theyson told me in a recent interview, that there was barely any conversation he can recollect at all.
"It's interesting," he said, when I enthusiastically asked about the chestplate imperialis, presumably while hammering the secret 'PR please get me away from this crazed nerd' button under his desk. "Actually I can't remember that we had the discussion, because I think we just took the latest iteration of them, and there it's black, right?"
"Dawn of War 1 is of course like our 'guiding star'," he continued, "but it's also like, 20 years old, right? And so a lot of stuff changed and happened, and so sometimes you have situations where you basically say, 'Okay, is this still a thing? Can we do this?' But in this case I think we just took the latest one." That latest one, as per the more recent White Dwarf edition, the somewhat niche Onslaught tabletop game, and the most recent video game in Dawn of War 3, was black.
There are other pressing questions, naturally. Some especially precise Space Marine fans have picked up on a specific phrase in the latest trailer, for instance. There, Blood Ravens Captain Cyrus refers to the Dark Angel who saved him as "brother". Technically - and this is getting a little niche even for me now - I gather that's a term Space Marines typically reserve for fellow chapter members, while members of other, allied ones get called something like "cousin". Does this mean the Dark Angels and Blood Ravens are related in some way, perhaps with a shared origin? Or is it just friendly chatter everybody's reading far too much into?
"In that case I can confirm it's just Space Marines who are 'brothers-in-arms'," Theysen smiled.
I dug a little more into the topic of the Blood Ravens' origins, just in case. In terms of their background, Theysen said "it's not going to be a huge part [of the game], because they're very far from home and on the wrong side of the Great Rift and so on. So for them, it's more about survival basically. And so it's not exploring their history, and they're not going back to their old world or anything like that."
That's three-for-three on my lore fishing attempts, so one more for luck. One popular, albeit slightly far-fetched fan theory as to the Blood Ravens' origins has been to speculate that they might share a gene seed with the Thousand Sons, a corrupted Chaos Legion with a similar colour scheme, similar mottos, and similarly unusual number of psykers in their armies.
There's no confirmed mention of Chaos being a faction in Dawn of War 4 so far, playable or otherwise. But do the Thousand Sons get a mention at all?
Read into that what you will. My interpretation: maybe lore needs a rule of cool, too.
In the meantime, look out for a slightly less ridiculous conversation between myself and Theysen, as well as more detailed thoughts on my latest time with the game, here on Eurogamer soon.

item.description:
I, for my sins, enjoy parry mechanics. I use 'parry slop' lovingly as a shorthand to refer to action games I want to play which feature parrying as a predominant mechanic. I am also a Call of Duty campaign enjoyer, and those games rarely feature any melee combat, let alone something as advanced as parrying. So, to say I was genuinely surprised to see Modern Warfare 4 bring the two together would be an understatement.
Yes, that's right. In case you haven't jumped into the Modern Warfare 4 campaign early, it has lengthy segments where your only weapon is your fists. In fact, those hand-to-hand encounters can only be finished by learning the parry timing; whiff it or mess it up, and it's an insta-Game Over. You've been able to punch people in COD campaigns before, of course, but none have the depth - or frequency - seen in Infinity Ward's latest. We're first introduced to the idea in the second mission, but that version is elementary compared to what's thrown at you later.
Out in the Cold, the earlier mission, actually starts out as more of a play on John Wick. Price, dressed in plain clothes, enters a nightclub looking for a lead on a target. Things quickly escalate - as they tend to do in MW campaigns - and Price finds himself pushing through a packed nightclub with nothing but a handgun. As it goes, the John Wick inspirations become clearer with a shootout in one of those rooms with anamorphic 3D LED light walls.
The game's hand-to-hand tech is introduced when a security guard attempts to stop you. To my knowledge, this is the first time I've seen the prompt 'Block just before being hit to parry' in a COD campaign. The game slows down time to let you read it and internalise the concept, but not nearly long enough for me to pick my jaw off the floor.
I decided to test the depth of the mechanic with the next opponent and wasn't impressed: guards have limited animations and wide attack windows that were easy to read. Deeper into the mission, however, enemies start adding mix-ups (!) into their repertoire, culminating with a multi-stage fight against a boss who introduces knives (harder to parry) into the formula, before throwing kicks and back-handed punches into the mix after you disarm him.
The game never shows stamina or stagger gauges, which - ironically - adds more depth to the system. You're forced to read attack animations to be able to time your block and land the parry. Without parrying, you simply can't break your opponent's posture and perform a takedown, you have to participate in the dance in order to advance.
There are a few of these throughout the Modern Warfare 4 campaign, but none more impressive than a pivotal fight in the latter half of the game. On top of standard punches, knife attacks and kicks, your opponents can now perform headbutts. This is made more impressive by their ability to dodge, a move you do not have access to.
There's a surprisingly dense animation system that makes all of that work. Hits are sharp, delivered with a heft and weight games don't get right often. There are even bespoke knife parry animations that play when your knife connects with the opponent's. If you were feeling generous, you could call it COD's version of Onimusha's steel-on-steel combat, I suppose.
So, have we reached peak parry slop? No! Parrying adds depth to what would otherwise be mundane moments. More games can be enriched by borrowing mechanics from popular genres outside their own. Call of Duty has actually been doing more of that in recent years, expanding campaigns to include loot, crafting, and open-world scavenging mechanics. They're not always done well, but when they are, they create memorable moments that go beyond breaking up the pace.
Now, I want to know if the same hand-to-hand system has carried over to DMZ. Imagine the possibilities!

item.title: Microsoft has revealed the second batch of games coming to Xbox Game Pass this month, and there are few genuine corkers, including the console debuts of The Séance of Blake Manor and Mouthwashing, and the addition of Final Fantasy 7 Remake Intergrade - which only arrived on Xbox earlier this year. item.description:
Microsoft has revealed the second batch of games coming to Xbox Game Pass this month, and there are few genuine corkers, including the console debuts of The Séance of Blake Manor and Mouthwashing, and the addition of Final Fantasy 7 Remake Intergrade - which only arrived on Xbox earlier this year.
The Séance of Blake Manor, a supernatural detective mystery, was released last year on PC. It casts you as a man sent to investigate the disappearance of a young woman in a remote part of Ireland in 1879 - a man who sees more than most people would, for both better and worse. Matt Wales described it as a "fantastically atmospheric" and "incredibly tense" adventure when he wrote about The Séance of Blake Manor last year, and Blake Manor finished as our 19th favourite game of 2025 in our big, annual list.
Mouthwashing, meanwhile, is a first-person horror with a PS1-style retro aesthetic, that tells a time-hopping story aboard a ship travelling through space. "Mouthwashing is a wildly inventive horror game that plays with the boundaries of time and space to exhilarating effect, and all with a gleeful glint in its large and unblinking eyeball," wrote Katherine in our Mouthwashing review.
Final Fantasy 7 Remake Intergrade - an enhanced version of the first part of the Remake trilogy - was originally released in 2021, so its Xbox and Switch arrival earlier this year was a long time coming. Nevertheless, the FF7 Remake remains excellent, even if it's starting to show its age, as Alex Donaldson argued.
A fresh wave of games also means some games are leaving Xbox Game Pass. Notable leavers include Lucasarts games Day of the Tentacle Remastered and Grim Fandango Remastered, as well as co-op game Deep Rock Galactic.
To see all the games currently available on Xbox Game Pass, check our big, regularly pruned list.

item.title: Subnautica 2 has begun its "voyage to Early Access 2.0", developer Unknown Worlds has said, with the revelation of a new update containing the "scariest" region they've ever made for the underwater game. Delightful. Read more
item.description:
Subnautica 2 has begun its "voyage to Early Access 2.0", developer Unknown Worlds has said, with the revelation of a new update containing the "scariest" region they've ever made for the underwater game. Delightful.
In a video released on the Subnautica YouTube channel, creative director Anthony Gallegos said the new update features multiple new biomes within the spooky region, and includes story additions, new Leviathan behaviors, and a Frog chassis for the tadpole submersible. In short, it's a pilotable mech.
In addition, the ability to dash underwater has been added when wearing fins. This means that players wearing them can quickly propel themselves forward with the press of a button. Previously, this was only available via a biomod - a player upgrade - so this change should make navigation a whole lot easier.
There are also new building options for your base, including a round room, but further details will have to wait, to be revealed in the coming months, through deep dive videos - get it? - on the individual changes.
An actual date for this "Early Access 2.0" release has not been revealed, and no scheduled window has been hinted at as of writing. Nonetheless, it marks a substantial suite of updates to the popular survival adventure game, which launched to substantial success earlier this year.
The game was also at the heart of a legal battle between the founders of Unknown Worlds and Krafton's CEO, who clashed over a hefty $250m bonus package based on the success of the game. Following this hubbub, Krafton said it wanted to turn Subnautica into a "franchise IP", just as Subnautica 2 passed the 5 million sales milestone.

item.title: You can play Football Manager 27 on PC and Mac for free this year for five full days later this month, in a first for the series and apparently an "industry first" for games of its kind. Read more
item.description:
You can play Football Manager 27 on PC and Mac for free this year for five full days later this month, in a first for the series and apparently an "industry first" for games of its kind.
The free period itself will start on 29th October at 6pm GMT, and run until its typical paid 'launch preview' period starts on the 3rd November, which is available to those who pre-order the game before its full launch on 10th November.
"Making an annual title free to play with all game modes available is believed to be an industry first and is a move that continues Sports Interactive's efforts to support its community of players," a studio press release says.
FM27's pre-orders, meanwhile, will then only open alongside the free play period, where players can buy with a 10 percent discount to get access to the aforementioned launch preview. Your saves will also continue across all of these periods into the full game, which is a nice touch, and likewise for those playing on Xbox Game Pass, too.
The news comes in an unusually quiet pre-launch period for developer Sports Interactive, and after the especially rough year of FM26, which despite steady player numbers still sits at a 'Mostly Negative' Steam user score, almost a full year after its launch.
That game was the first in two years, after Sports Interactive took the extraordinary step of cancelling the release of FM25 while it moved the game over to the Unity game engine from its own internal one. The result was new systems that the developer says weren't possible in previous versions of the game - notably the quite sophisticated system of splitting out in- and out-of-possession formations and tactics - at the expense of a huge number of classic features the developer couldn't get working in time. That, and a reworked "cards and tiles" user interface that I and an awful lot of players found a bit of a nightmare to navigate.
It all makes for a huge year for the franchise. FM27 promises "an improved interface with more intuitive navigation, creating a more immersive experience," as well as several new features such as Tactical Tweaks, which supplement the old, returning touchline shouts system. Whether they come off is likely to have a major impact on fans' trust in the studio after a difficult couple of years. This five-day free period at least suggests Sports Interactive is feeling confident.

item.title: Xbox is reportedly gearing up for three more rounds of layoffs as the Microsoft gaming division continues CEO Asha Sharma's plan to reset the business. According to a new report, the first of these is taking place this month, followed by another in November and one in January 2027. Read more
item.description:
Xbox is reportedly gearing up for three more rounds of layoffs as the Microsoft gaming division continues CEO Asha Sharma's plan to reset the business. According to a new report, the first of these is taking place this month, followed by another in November and one in January 2027.
That's according to "people familiar with the plans", who revealed that to Fortune Magazine in a new report which also featured a profile of Sharma. Plans could change, however, the people said.
If true, this would be the second round in as many months, following September's round which saw the elimination of 268 roles alongside organisational changes that moved Obsidian under Bethesda, with Rare and World's Edge joining Activision.
Those layoffs are part of what's considered the second major wave in Xbox's larger plan to cut costs and return the division to profitability. The first wave was the largest by far. It took place in July and saw over 1,600 job cuts. The remaining 1,600 are planned to be distributed across future quarters, culminating in the early months of 2027.
Thanks to this latest report, we now know when those remaining cuts will occur. The report does not offer any information on which teams are in Sharma's crosshairs, considering the massive cuts that already took place at its largest and most iconic studios.
One of the biggest remaining question marks, however, surrounds the fate of Gears of War: E-Day studio The Coalition. The Canadian first-party studio just released the third-person shooter to what appears to be softer than anticipated sales.
Eurogamer spoke to members of The Coalition's development team as they were preparing to release E-Day, and it's clear there's widespread worry Xbox will reduce staff at the studio now that their latest project has shipped. Many also fear the cuts could be timed in such a way to prevent those potentially getting laid off from receiving promised bonuses.
We're well over halfway through October, so if the information is accurate, the bad news is likely to be announced this week or next. The same report also revealed that Xbox is internally estimating next-gen Helix consoles to cost between $1,200 and $1,800.

item.title: Physical disc-based copies of Resident Evil: Requiem on PlayStation consoles may have been more popular than all versions of the game on Xbox, a new report has found, while unearthing a trove of other statistics about physical sales. Read more
item.description:
Physical disc-based copies of Resident Evil: Requiem on PlayStation consoles may have been more popular than all versions of the game on Xbox, a new report has found, while unearthing a trove of other statistics about physical sales.
Meanwhile, physical sales of 007 First Light, Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced, and Crimson Desert are all under 30 percent of their relevant totals, according to this report. This makes physical sales a minority, but if the figures are accurate, proves that they still account for a hearty chunk of the total revenue for these single-player games. Wolverine, another example used by Rhys, seems to owe 800,000 of its 2.6m sales to physical copies, as well as nearly a third of its total revenue.
In Japan, there's even stronger support for physical game sales. First-party PlayStation and Japan-centric games such as Capcom releases tend to sell more physical copies there. have a larger slice of its total sales be physical than other types of games.
Elliott surmises that's because physical games are more "ingrained in the culture" there. 44 percent of Pragmata's copies sold were physical, for example, and 44.1 percent of Onimusha: Way of the Sword's sales were physical too. With Japan responsible for 12 percent of Onimusha's sales and 11 percent of Pragmata's, the nation's buying habits are enough to make a substantial impact on global statistics.
It's against that backdrop that the new, digital-only and Japan-exclusive PS5 Black has launched in Japan, for $350, with a separate disc drive sold for $75. Elliott interprets this as an attempt to "nudge" Japanese users towards buying games digitally.
However, whereas physical sales for single-player games seem healthy, it's a different situation for sports games. PlayStation's current top-selling game - FC 27 - owes only 8.9 percent of its sales to physical. Still, as is noted by Elliott, the relative popularity of physical games on PlayStation is likely a key component of the backlash Sony has faced with its decision to shift towards digital.
Only Monday, PlayStation founder Ken Kutaragi said that discs became a "metaphor for 'owning' games", and that the upset at their discontinuation was probably a "mentality issue". Sony has also pledged to continue its plans to move away from discs despite the associated outrage.

item.title: The price of Xbox's next generation console, codename Project Helix, may be higher than many of us expected. Helix, which is reportedly going to ship as two devices, is estimated to cost close to $2,000. Read more
item.description:
The price of Xbox's next generation console, codename Project Helix, may be higher than many of us expected. Helix, which is reportedly going to ship as two devices, is estimated to cost close to $2,000.
That's according to a wide-ranging new report and profile of Xbox CEO Asha Sharma by Fortune Magazine. In it, it's claimed Xbox's internal estimates have arrived at a staggering price: between $1,200 (~£900) and $1,800 (~£1,345). This is not simply the cost of components and manufacturing, it's the price Xbox reportedly expects the console to cost consumers, assuming it is not subsidised.
The report also revealed that Helix, which Sharma previously stressed is a family of devices, will indeed encompass two consoles: a traditional box and a handheld. Xbox is reportedly planning to release the handheld Helix first, with the current target being holiday 2027. The main, under-the-tv box Helix is instead planned for holiday 2028.
As shocking as these prices may be, they're not entirely out of line with what industry insiders have been saying we should expect. The global AI-driven memory and storage shortage has caused prices of practically all consumer electronics to shoot up significantly. The shortages also resulted in Xbox, PlayStation and Nintendo all raising prices of their years-old current-gen consoles on multiple occasions since their launches.
The flagship Xbox Series X, which launched at $500 / £450, now costs $800 / £670. The Series S, initially pitched as a budget-friendly, entry level console now costs $500 / £430, up from $300 / £250. A Helix console at $1,200 would mean a 50 percent increase on top of Series X's current price.
The report also revealed an internal divide between the Xbox and Windows teams over which operating system handheld Helix should run. Microsoft's Windows team reportedly wanted a slimmed down version of Windows Home to run on the handheld, whereas the Xbox team instead wanted specialised software to maximise gaming performance.
The disagreements reportedly got so bad that an Xbox executive threatened to end the handheld project entirely. It's not clear what the big-box Helix is going to run, however, seeing as it was envisioned as a bridge between PC and Xbox capable of playing games from both platforms.

item.title: A former long-time Call of Duty developer has called out Activision executives profiteering from the re-release of games like Black Ops 1 and 2, whereas the developers who contributed "blood, sweat, and tears" to make them gained nothing. Read more
item.description:
A former long-time Call of Duty developer has called out Activision executives profiteering from the re-release of games like Black Ops 1 and 2, whereas the developers who contributed "blood, sweat, and tears" to make them gained nothing.
Gavin Goslin worked at Treyarch for more than 15 years as a level artist and level designer, and in a LinkedIn post reacting to low effort re-releases of Black Ops 1 & 2 this year, said: "They are printing money off of work completed over a decade ago.
"As a developer who actually worked on both BO1 and BO2, seeing these charts is bittersweet. I poured my life into those games, spending countless, brutal hours in crunch alongside an incredibly talented team to make sure they were perfect. Seeing our blood, sweat, and tears still dominating the charts in 2026 is amazing, but it's hard to watch the suits rake in giant financial windfalls from our old code while the actual creators don't see a dime of it."
The post was subsequently picked up by various gaming websites - a recirculation Goslin reacted to in a separate post on LinkedIn today. "I am glad this critical conversation is gaining traction," Goslin said.
"To watch executives rake in massive financial windfalls off our old code, while the actual creators face unemployment and don't see a dime of that new compensation, highlights a fundamental flaw in how our industry values its talent," Goslin added. "If legacy games are going to print money for publishers in 2026, legacy rewards and protections need to exist for the developers who survived the crunch to build them."
The Call of Duty: Black Ops 1 & 2 re-releases, released in July, were reportedly a huge success for Activision and owner Microsoft, selling something like 11 million copies and raking in nearly $450m. This is despite the fact they are not remasters but simple re-releases. US data-tracker Circana not only highlighted Black Ops 1 & 2 as the highest earning game in July, but called it the fifth highest-earning game of the year. It's a remarkable success for simply re-issuing these roughly 15-year-old games.
Meanwhile, the new Call of Duty game, Modern Warfare 4, prepares for release this Friday, 23rd October, buoyed by a very positive reaction to its campaign, by players with pre-order early access to the game. We're in the process of reviewing the game and will share our thoughts soon.

item.title: Helldivers will be switching up its anti-cheat, as developer Arrowhead Game Studios has admitted that its Gameguard cheat policy "wasn't as effective as it could have been." Read more
item.description:
Helldivers will be switching up its anti-cheat, as developer Arrowhead Game Studios has admitted that its Gameguard cheat policy "wasn't as effective as it could have been."
In a post made to the game's Steam page (not available in the UK - get that VPN on), the team explains the decision: "The implementation of GameGuard for Helldivers 2 wasn't as effective as it could have been [...] In the end we decided to take another path with EAC. EAC is an industry standard used in over 200 games, and we believe this will be an effective way to protect the Galactic War and will better protect fair gameplay and the integrity of the game."
As part of this shift, Arrowhead also confirmed that several non-malicious mods, such as cosmetic changes, will need to be updated to work alongside Easy Anti-Cheat. "We know mods are part of the DNA of PC gaming and gaming communities as a whole. In general, we appreciate the creativity behind cosmetic and non-gameplay mods, which players can enjoy without negatively impacting those who play alongside them," the post reads.
"Where we need to improve is how we protect players against modifications that create unfair advantages or negatively impact others, which goes beyond software manipulation to tamper with our game. These changes mean that some mods, particularly the types that are affecting the experience of other players, may no longer function."
The post continues to implore those who feel a non-malicious mod has been blocked by Easy Anti-Cheat to reach out via Zendesk. So, there should be a bit of a rough transitional period, but hopefully a lot of the fun mods should be good to go again in the near future.
It's indeed true that Easy Anti-Cheat has become the norm for a vast variety of PC games. However, regardless of the anti cheat being used, those in the UK are still unable to play Helldivers 2 due to a mysterious issue. Sony has promised to address the issue with Valve, but as of writing there's been no resolution to the problem.
