item.description:
One of my very favourite things to do in Switch Sports Resort isn't, technically, a sport at all. I can't get enough of Prop Plane's free-play mode, taking to the skies, and watching Wuhu Island do its thing below. Swing past the art museum or the shopping precinct and you'll see all sorts of little people milling around; take a wrong-way dive into a tunnel and here come the cars whizzing on by. Out on the water, racers whip and twirl; on the archipelago's sandiest beaches, holidayers recline in the tropical sun. Fly over the stadiums and sports arenas and you'll see matches in progress - furious bouts of tennis, concentrated swings on golfing greens, or the pin-toppling bustle of bowling - crowds going wild in tandem. And if it's quieter contemplation I want, I can explore the subterranean depths of a volcano, or chart a gently winding path along the river banks, or admire the lighthouse perched on the hill.
It's all so extra; a big, characterful backdrop full of lovely little flourishes that bleed into the games themselves. From the crowds milling lazily along the beach behind the table tennis arena as boats drift on by, to the lovable daftness of it all, as players make hyperkinetic slapstick dashes across tennis courts or glower with teeth-gritted fury in between boxing match rounds. It's just very Nintendo; packed with endlessly delightful incidental touches that help massively elevate what is, in essence, a relatively straightforward and largely familiar collection of sports-themed mini-games. And fundamentally Switch Sports Resort really is more of the same; albeit a further evolution of the hugely influential Wii Sports formula that here, fourth time around, is perhaps at its most refined.
Switch Sports Resort brings together a total of 12 activities (13 if you count the rope-jump "warm-up"), and, shorn of its predecessors' filler, it's a strong line-up. You've got four bona fide classics in returning Wii Sports favourites Tennis, Golf, Bowling, and Boxing; five from 2009's Wii Sports Resort (Archery, Basketball, Table Tennis, Power Cruising, and Prop Plane), plus three new additions in Thumb Wrestling, Volleyball, and Skateboarding; all intuitively adapted for Switch 2's responsive motion controls. And the balance between accessibility and depth feels right. This is a game that favours quickfire arcade-y immediacy over fussy simulation, but still manages to capture the essence of each sport. And as easy to learn as most games are, there's enough subtlety beneath the slapstick silliness to create space for skill, and they adapt equally well to impromptu family chaos and more focused play.
The Big Four - Bowling, Boxing, Golf, and Tennis - are, of course, classics for a reason, and they're still winners here. Tennis and Bowling remain the gold standard; the kind of games you can shove into anyone's hand and they'll have a good time, instinctively picking up the nuances of each, the curves and the angles, as they go along (Table Tennis is similarly approachable, although its comparative restraint - trading the giddying arm flails of its bigger brother for subtler wrist action - is a slightly harder sell). Golf and Boxing are a touch more involved - boxing with its upper and lower cuts, its dodge timings and stamina management; golf with its reliance on an on-screen power meter that requires splitting your focus in two - but those hurdles are easily surmountable. And Golf, in particular, with its leisurely pace and less frenetic competition remains a unique sort of low-key thrill.
Archery, too, is a blast; its two controller set-up - one for the bow, the other the string - wonderfully mimicking the act of launching an arrow as you pull back, take aim, and fire. Thumb Wrestling is perhaps the dark horse of the bunch; a deceptively simple game of pin-the-digit that quickly descends into psychological warfare as you embark on an increasingly desperate succession of frantic shake-offs and sneaky feints. As for the final two competitive sports on the roster, Basketball and Volleyball, I'm not so keen. Break them down to their constituent parts, and the moment-by-moment movements - the shooting, the dribbling, the jumps, and the bumps - translate well to motion controls. It's just that in trying to adapt both games into something manageably quickfire, it all feels a little awkward - each defensive and offensive phase requiring its own moves you'll switch between when told like a game of Simon Says. There's no real sense of fluidity and momentum, nor are they easy to explain for casual play.
But actually, it doesn't really matter. Basketball and Volleyball, like most games in the pack, come with some properly enjoyable variants, spinning the core of the sport into something new. Basketball's frantic single-player hoop-shooting variant is a brilliantly breathless dash against the clock, for instance, while Volleyball gets a rhythm-action twist, requiring players to bop balls on beat, listening for tricksy musical cues that gets increasingly chaotic as things go on. Bowling, meanwhile, offers the classic 100-pin variant and a fun mini-golf-like spin that challenges players to hit pins while navigating shifting obstacles, massive gaps, and bizarrely undulating lanes. And I particularly adore Archery's special rules. Here, players score points by landing an arrow on a shared target; hit a competitor's area instead of your own, however, and they get the points. More points are earned closer to the bullseye where all quadrants converge, making for some nailbiting risk and reward. Another twist: the better you do, the smaller your quadrant gets, and then come the moving targets and high winds. It's a load of fun.
Not every sport and every variant supports four players on a single console (Nintendo, incidentally, has done a decent job of streamlining controller requirements, so you'll generally only need one pair of Joy-Cons for two players, and two sets for four), and not everything is playable online. But online play - from the admittedly small amount of time I've had to muck around with it - feels robust, and a fine way to expand Switch Sports Resort's longevity and appeal. Up to eight people can join an online friend lobby, with two players supported per console. Up to two players can also join random matchmaking online, and here, you've got options: ranked play is limited to the standard sports rules and gradually adjusts your grade as you win or lose matches, influencing who you're paired with next. Casual play, meanwhile, pairs you with randoms for an unranked free-for-all. You can toggle the sports you want to get involved in, and it's here you might stumble across online versions of those special rules.
Actually, probably the biggest surprise of Switch Sports Resort - given the series' party game legacy - is just how much I've enjoyed playing solo. Online play might not have the same chaotic allure as playing in person, but it still offers a compellingly competitive thrill. GameChat is supported for friends list communication, while a cute sticker system lets you furiously emote with strangers (my personal favourite: sad dinosaur). And there are loose progression systems pulling you onward too. Island Crown mode, for instance, pits you against 20 increasingly challenging opponents in each sport without needing to go online. And there's a big long list of achievements for specific activities, alongside more general, esoteric ones. The implementation of achievements is a touch awkward, mind - in order to claim the cosmetic rewards and points associated with them, you'll have to squirrel around in submenus - but it's still an enjoyable bit of something extra for completionists to work toward. And yes, points.
Pretty much everything you do - from simply participating in a game to performing some specific in-match feat - earns you points, both on- and offline. Points, in turn, can be spent in the shop, unlocking cosmetics that range from avatar clothing and nameplate backgrounds to alternate bits of sports equipment and stickers. And there's some cool stuff! Right now I'm rocking those dinosaur emojis and a spooky werebear hat. I don't love the FOMO tricks on display here (there are daily log-in bonuses, weekly and monthly cosmetic set refreshes, and Gacha-style random drops), but it's hardly egregious. Points are generously doled out, sets are easy to complete, and there's no real-world money involved. And if this keeps players engaged and the online community healthy, then I guess okay - I certainly wouldn't have put in so much online time if I wasn't so desperate for those dinosaur stickers!
It's just a shame the vast majority of cosmetic clothing only works with Nintendo's Sportsmates avatars, leaving (the thankfully still supported) Miis a poor second. The cosmetics are great, but the Sportsmates still look off to me; weirdly soulless creations, with limited facial customisation options, that feel like they've just stumbled in from some lesser Wii-era party game.
There are, of course, three sports I haven't yet talked about, all falling under the umbrella of what Nintendo calls "leisure" games. These are the ones that best showcase Wuhu Island's open-world design and they're brilliant things. Skateboarding is the clear standout, and might well be my favourite of the entire package. It's played using Switch 2's mouse mode configuration, Joy-Con flat on a surface, as you pull back to gather speed, flick to jump, and tilt to steer. I LOVE it. It's wonderfully responsive and surprisingly invigorating as you careen around Wuhu Island, the haptic rumble of wheels-on-tarmac perfectly completing the illusion.
As with Switch Sports Resort's other two leisure offerings, you can skateboard in a number of ways. There's an enjoyably relaxed free-play mode, letting you explore the island with no time limit; a sightseeing mode, which sees you scrambling against the clock to find photo spots and other craftily hidden knick-knacks to tick off your missions list, either playing alone or competitively. There's also an enormously entertaining set of curated tracks that can be played as competitive races or solo time trials.
Power Cruising offers the similar amusements, albeit shifted to the water. And while its controls are likely to be divisive - its tilt-your-body set-up feels just a bit too much for these old bones - its Wave-Race-style frollicking is still a fun time. And then, of course, there's Prop Plane, where you intuitively tilt your controller like a paper aircraft as you glide serenely through the skies. Poor old Prop Plane, though, doesn't get any racing - not even a couple of Pilotwings-style fly-through-the-rings challenges - and is instead lumbered with a rather half-arsed competitive balloon-collecting mode. And, honestly, as enjoyable as the open-world stuff frequently is, it's hard not to feel a touch disappointed too. For starters, you can't play leisure sports online outside of friend lobbies, but more than that, Wuhu Island is such an engaging space to tootle around, it's a shame not to see Nintendo make more of it - even 2009's Wii Sports Resort had multiple aeronautical activities that would have been welcome additions here.
Grumbles aside, though, Switch Sports Resort is a bit of a gem. It's perhaps the series' most refined entry yet; bundling up a bunch of genuine crowd-pleasers in a charmingly sunkissed, wonderfully considered package that's equally suited to online and solo play. It's perfectly timed to become a family mainstay as the festivities set in, but the biggest surprise for me is how easily it's slipped into my own rotation; how often I've found myself firing it up for a quick blast of casual online chaos between other things, or to hit the golfing green when I'm in a more laidback frame of mind. And as I'm inevitably drawn to the skies once more - Wuhu Island's swaying palms, sandy beaches, and tropical waters stretching out before me - it really does feel like a jolly holiday compared to the grim wintery greyness beyond my rain-spattered window.
A copy of Nintendo Switch Sports Resort was provided for this review by Nintendo.

item.description:
I think the most memorable bit of brilliance in the otherwise flawed diamond that is Final Fantasy 16 is the way it handles legacy. There are moments where Clive and his recalcitrant band of revolutionaries rage against the way of the world: they burn down cities, depose oligarchs, shatter crystals. It's a none-too-subtle rallying cry against the binding nature of tradition: a radical plea to tear down the structures of the past in order to sow the seeds of the future.
It reflects a game that, as the most recent numbered entry in the series, also feels like an awkward teenager unsure of its place in the grandiose canon of its heritage. But Final Fantasy Resonance doesn't have that problem; it's not thrashing against the constraints of its maker, growling and grumbling bitterly as it desperately tries to break out of that Final Fantasy-shaped box it's been shoved into. Rather, Resonance is the other side of the same coin; trying too hard to live up to, emulate, mimic what came before. And that equal obsession with legacy carries similar consequences for this young upstart as it did its grizzled older sibling.
One of the most essential elements to a Final Fantasy game is its story. Even from the early days when a desperado company on the edge of bankruptcy threw caution to the wind to make the singular game it wanted to play, assuming it'd be its final hurrah - its 'final' fantasy - the series has had an obsession with storytelling. And rightly so; the brazen, often quite nonsensical plots of Hironobu Sakaguchi, Yoshinori Kitase, Kazushige Nojima, Daisuke Watanabe, and way more besides often get quite cumbersome. Amnesia, time travel, multi-dimensional rifts, patriarchal space whales - you name it, this series has had it.
Resonance, puffing up its chest as it stands in line next to its esteemed siblings, tries hard to fit in, but in doing so picks up all these tropes without really understanding why they (kind-of) work in those other games. So you're left with a grab-bag of nonsense; mages that don't know who they are, spunky swordsmen that hate their dads, reticent loners that walk the path of the blade, womanising mercenaries fighting for the fate of a nation… it's all a bit much. And I say that as someone with a high tolerance for 'anime nonsense' in my role-playing games.
I think my main issue with the story and cast of Resonance lies in how shallow it all feels. The cast has no chemistry. Plot points just happen, with no real time to digest or feel the impact in the world. One mission sees an entire city swallowed by floodwater, only for everything to go back to normal once you've solved the inciting incident. Can you imagine that in FF7 or FF8 - if the slums barely reacted to the falling of the Sector 7 plate, or none of the characters really noticed what happened to Trabia Garden?
This sense of worldly stasis comes from how Resonance has been reanimated, I think: it began life as a doomed mobile game, Final Fantasy Brave Exvius, its story stripped out of season one and shunted into Resonance. The graphics, battle system, and some key mechanics were altered - improved, actually - but the story… It is, by far, the weakest facet. Things, which feels almost obligatory to say for this series, get better about 30 hours in, but given it's also only 30-40 hours long (unless you're sniffing out all the open-world side missions) that does little to allay how boring the overall plot feels, and how frustratingly over-written it is in the moment-to-moment. Using cool words like 'puissance' means very little if the standard back-and-forth is chittering nonsense, I'm afraid!
At least Resonance is generous when it comes to battles. Many will argue that a good, emotive story is the backbone of the Final Fantasy series, but I actually think it's the battle mechanics that have kept SquareSoft/Square Enix's storied series alive for the last 40 years. From the traditional turn-based epoch of FF1 through FF3, the 'active-time battle' experiments of FF4 through 9, the unbeatable 'conditional turn battles' of FF10, and all the weird and wonderful mixes that came after, Final Fantasy is no stranger to probing how we play. So it should be galling seeing Resonance fall back into old habits, but instead the resultant battle mechanic is compelling and hard to put down.
Resonance uses a mix of the synergy/stamina setup from FF13, 15 and the 7 Remake series, alongside a more traditional turn-based system that - actually - is more like something from Octopath Traveler than any numbered FF entry (and that's notable, given how Octopath 0 also rejigged a dead mobile game into a somewhat successful 'full game' release). Here, enemies are furnished with a HP and a stamina bar. Whittling down HP kills them, but emptying their stamina interrupts attacks, puts them into a 'stagger' state that causes them to soak up more damage, and allows your party to take a bonus turn. In the bonus phase, certain skills gain additional effects, and it all ends with the option to summon a 'vision' - a bonus character from the depths of the series' long history - to perform a big attack that does ample damage and can confer bonus effects to the allied party.
It sounds complicated - and it is when all the pistons are firing in unison - but because Resonance takes over 10 hours to really start up its engines, you're able to pilot it all quite naturally as the interlocking elements are gradually introduced. Mob enemies are felled easily enough - though there are those who'll hobble you - and bosses are common enough to keep you on your toes as you hunt down 'visions' to open up your strategic choices, and level up your company to keep you battle-ready as the world gets harder and uglier around you.
Bosses, especially those that end each of Resonance's eight chapters, are highlights. Even if you're overleveled, they can be surprisingly hard if you don't engage with the stagger, 'vision', and RPG mechanics, and I feel that for every complaint I have about the characters and world-building of Resonance, I've got a counter-argument when it comes to its battles: I love how punishing it can be; I love how much stat buffs and debuffs matter (it's not quite Shin Megami Tensei-level, but it's not far off!); I love the weird and wonderful mechanics that start to crop up when a certain character joins your crew in Chapter 4, and I love how many potential builds there are with certain 'visions' equipped to different characters.
Final Fantasy Resonance producer Keisuke Nakashima has gone on record saying the game's combat is largely inspired by FF5 and FF6, and you can see that: the 'visions' sort of work as a proxy for FF5's still best-in-class job system, whereas each individual character has their own strengths and unique abilities, as the core cast did in FF6. It's a wondrous combination, and something I genuinely hope inspires whatever comes next for either the main series, or whatever other side projects this team cooks up in the Final Fantasy canon.
As is the case with so many Final Fantasy games, everything exhales when you get the airship - the open world actually becomes open, and side quests (which up until now have been arbitrary 'go here, do this' distractions) begin to matter. Exploration is rewarded with intriguing and weird hints about the state of the world. Peculiar new weapons make themselves known. You find a cave full of Marlboros. Little puzzles about hidden Espers start to appear. Your party fills out, and something clicks as you begin to understand the intended purpose for each character, and how previously unimportant 'visions' play into a wider strategy. This is peak Final Fantasy, eliciting the same feeling you get when reclaiming the Ragnarok in FF8, opening up the control panel for the Fahrenheit in FFX, or winning the Blackjack of Setzer in FF6.
Yes, the story steadfastly refuses to kick into gear, and there's some aggravating dungeon-design, but the latter half of Resonance still manages to be a riot, with its gauntlet of ever-escalating (and ever-interesting) boss fights. Resonance, playing up to its Final Fantasy inspirations, is even better in the final third - the world is your oyster, the impending threat of doom is just far enough away for you to enjoy soaking in the ambiance of a world on the edge of ruin, and each member of your team has settled into their tactical niche. You sort of don't want to hit the point of no return because here, at least, everything feels good.
Resonance is a decent game, a wonderful 'what if' experiment that asks 'what does a pixel-based Final Fantasy look like in 2026?' It's the best-looking HD-2D game I've ever played. It plays around with RPG combat mechanics in a way worthy of its esteemed series' inspirations. But some underwhelming world-building, a forgettable story, and pacing issues that feel egregious (even by some very relaxed genre standards) prevent it from ever feeling truly great - irrespective of how good those climactic battles feel. I can't help but wonder if Resonance would have been more successful if it ripped out its Brave Exvius history root-and-stem; replacing the episodic, gacha-supporting story with something more aligned with its 'full release' RPG aspirations. If you come to Final Fantasy for its emotive storytelling, memorable characters, and a complete world to get lost in, I think you'll leave disappointed. If you come looking for moreish, brain-scratching RPG combat puzzles, I couldn't recommend it more. It's a shame, really, that Resonance never quite gets to be more than the sum of its parts.

item.title: The Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 campaign is currently available in early access, and if you're among the many who pre-ordered a copy in order to play it before launch, you've likely noticed a locked difficulty setting that's harder, even, than Realism. Read more
item.description:
The Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 campaign is currently available in early access, and if you're among the many who pre-ordered a copy in order to play it before launch, you've likely noticed a locked difficulty setting that's harder, even, than Realism.
YOLO, which is short for you only live once, is a new difficulty tier introduced in Modern Warfare 4. It does exactly what you expect: gives you a single life to complete the entirety of the campaign. Die once and you're sent back to the start.
A few players have already cleared the Modern Warfare 4 campaign on YOLO, but one in particular took the time to answer a few questions and reveal some of their toughest moments in the campaign.
Reddit user Lost-Equivalent2352 shared a screenshot showing a completed campaign at YOLO difficulty, which they said took them 20 hours. Key to their strategy was, well, a lot of hiding and leaving AI teammates to kill as many enemies as possible, before emerging to finish the rest. They relied on flashbangs to momentarily stun enemies and make it easier to shoot them, but they also used a lot of grenades to clear clusters of enemies.
But that grenade strategy was difficult in one mission - a mission that depicts the chaos of a North Korean invasion of South Korea, and takes place at nighttime. The problem here is that civilians and other allies are spread across the battlefield, so throwing flashbangs and grenades risks damaging either group, ending the YOLO run. Lost-Equivalent2352 only managed to beat it by "pure luck", they said.
Incidentally, Lost-Equivalent2352 played the game using mouse and keyboard, saying: "I think that [it's] impossible to complete it with a controller, you need [good] recoil control in long distances but that's only my opinion."
According to Lost-Equivalent2352, the sections of hand-to-hand combat were among the most difficult, as miss-countering even a single attack can mean the end of the fight, which in turn means the end of the entire run. In those sections, you're unable to use anything but your fists, so there's really no getting around learning the fight.
In order to unlock YOLO, you must first finish the entire campaign on Realism difficulty, which is no easy feat. A YOLO run could end for any reason that shows a game over screen, including accidentally shooting a civilian, failing a jump, losing a chase and so on. Do any of that - or die normally - and you're back to the opening cutscene.
Given the single-life nature of the mode, you can't select missions individually and finish each on YOLO as you can with other difficulty levels, so you really have to do it the way it was intended.
Unfortunately, though, the reward for finishing the campaign on YOLO is underwhelming. It's a Calling Card you can use with your multiplayer profile. Calling Cards are amongst the lowest tier of cosmetic rewards in Call of Duty, so unless someone actually knows how it was acquired, most players probably won't notice.
Modern Warfare 4's DMZ early access begins later today, before the full game - including traditional multiplayer - launches Friday, 23rd October for PC, PS5, Xbox Series X/S and Switch 2.

item.title: PEGI, the European video game age rating agency, has started raising the age ratings of digital games that feature loot boxes to 16. The rollout of this new, stricter approach, is expected to occur throughout October. Read more
item.description:
PEGI, the European video game age rating agency, has started raising the age ratings of digital games that feature loot boxes to 16. The rollout of this new, stricter approach, is expected to occur throughout October.
The Games Rating Authority's Connor Hinde, announced the rollout on his personal LinkedIn. Hinde's post reads:
"Since June, newly submitted games have been assessed against an expanded set of criteria within the PEGI rating framework, including new criteria relating to interactive risks. As the UK administrator of PEGI, the Games Rating Authority has now begun applying these updated criteria to selected existing digital products.
"Existing digital-only games that are currently rated PEGI 3, 7 or 12 and feature Paid random items, such as loot boxes, will have their age rating updated to PEGI 16 – Paid random items."
This process began this week, and shall continue throughout the month. Hinde urged publishers or developers with questions or concerns to contact the PEGI helpdesk.
Games included in this policy change include ES Sports FC series, which previously was rated PEGI 3. Zenless Zone Zero, a gacha action game from HoYoVerse, has also seen its rating increase from a 12 to a 16 as a result of these shifting rules. Monopoly Go currently appears to still be rated as a 9+ on the Apple games store, though given its inclusion of randomised sticker packs and boxes it may well see its rating change.
Why does this matter? Well, it could signal to parents or potential players that a game's monetisation may not be appropriate for them or their loved ones. It is worth emphasising that this ruling impacts digital-only games, so it is largely up to parents to monitor the games their children are playing.
This shift follows the announcement back in March that PEGI would tackle games with loot boxes or similar microtransactions, addictive game mechanics, and unmonitored online communication. The agency has been working to better align itself with modern gaming practices for some time. With this rollout, it appears this effort is finally in effect.

item.title: UPDATE 21ST OCTOBER: This update has now been detailed by CD Projekt Red, and it's a big one, bringing dual-wielding, customisable cyberware, cross-platform mod support and more. Read more
item.description:
UPDATE 21ST OCTOBER: This update has now been detailed by CD Projekt Red, and it's a big one, bringing dual-wielding, customisable cyberware, cross-platform mod support and more.
ORIGINAL STORY 20th OCTOBER: CD Projekt Red has announced that Cyberpunk 2077 is getting a free update to coincide with the release of anime series Edgerunners 2 on Netflix.
Specifically, the new update is being released 22nd October on PC, PS5 and Xbox Series S/X - a Switch 2 version "will follow shortly", CDPR mentioned. The update is to "introduce a range of new items and features to the game, including content inspired by Cyberpunk: Edgerunners 2," CDPR said in a press release.
At the moment, there doesn't appear to be any more detail about the update to be had, though a livestream is planned for tomorrow, 21st October, at 5pm CEST (4pm BST), to detail what's in it.
The second season of Edgerunners is available to stream on Netflix now, and according to a review on our sister site IGN, is off to a tremendous start. The sentiment around the series was already strong from a very successful debut for Edgerunners a couple of years ago, and CDPR and animation studio Trigger appear to have built on that.
The renewed Cyberpunk activity is likely to have another bolstering effect on Cyberpunk 2077 sales, which earlier this year passed a remarkable 40 million-sold milestone. We'll bring you more details about the Cyberpunk update, and our thoughts on Edgerunners 2, as soon as we can.

item.description:
Red Dead Redemption 2's infamous animated horse testicles, which are realistic enough to contract in cold weather and expand again in the warmth, were apparently not a feature mandated by Rockstar. As iconic as they've become - a symbol of extraordinary detail in the game - they didn't originate from a list of features that needed to be added to the game. The horse testicles were instead the unexpected work of one person, or a group of people, autonomously working on the Cowboy epic.
Journalist Jason Schreier heard this anecdote from Rockstar head of development Aaron Garbut while visiting Rockstar North to write an expansive report for Bloomberg about the making of GTA 6. "Garbut actually brought this up," Schreier said in a video on YouTube. "[The horse testicles were] not something that was on some big list of features to make; it was not something that an art director told an artist, 'Alright, we've got to get those horse testicles in here - better put in nights and weekends so you can get these horse testicles in here.'
"That was something that people, or a person on their own, autonomously decided, 'OK, I'm going to do this because I think it's a really cool detail and I have enough time to work on it." We're checking the veracity of this anecdote with Rockstar, by the way.
And that anecdote is important because it relates to another thing Schreier was told by Garbut, which was that no one person at Rockstar knows everything that's in GTA 6 because it's too big and detailed to do that. "There's no one person that has this whole thing in their head," Garbut apparently said.
That, coupled with the fact that developers apparently have "autonomy to put in things that are cool", Schreier said, means there could be another unexpected feature like horse testicles in GTA 6. And given the nudity-related GTA 6 video leaks we've already had, perhaps the features aren't that far removed.
Schreier's video revealed a few other tidbits of information learnt on his trip to Rockstar. He was told that roads in GTA 6 are "significantly narrower" than in GTA 5, apparently, so players feel the effects of traffic more - a detail that relates to the increased levels of realism in GTA 6.
He also heard how some artists had been working on GTA 6 for 11 years, and whereas there were "five of six" people in GTA 5's art production team, there were - or are - 65 people in GTA 6's art production team. Note that Rockstar, as a company, has roughly doubled in size since the release of 2018's Red Dead Redemption 2, growing from 2,441 employees to 4,711 across 12 offices.
There's also some information about the origins of the contextual 'hold left trigger' interaction system introduced in Red Dead Redemption 2, which again, apparently came from someone autonomously working on the game - Phil Hooker (now director of technology) - rather than from one of the game's creative leads. Also, many experiments were apparently done to find a replacement for GTA's radial menu but in the end, the team reverted back to it.
Grand Theft Auto 6 is, of course, releasing a month from now on 19th November. The road to launch has been bumpy, however, with Rockstar North currently embroiled in an employment tribunal in Scotland over the alleged unjust firings of 31 employees, and with a series of gameplay footage leaks exposing GTA 6 in ways that are outside of Rockstar's control.

item.description:
Bungie surprised players last month by announcing its intention to bring back Destiny 2 campaigns and other additions taken out of the game over the years. When that 'unvaulting' plan was initially announced, Bungie didn't share any specifics, nor a timeline as to when we can expect the things to return.
Now, the developer is finally offering some hints. Bungie head of product, Josh Deane, revealed that Bungie is close to sharing a progress update. "I know there are a lot of questions on the how, what, when of unvaulting. Including any potential future updates to D2 and what's beyond for Destiny," Deane wrote on X in a post only recently spotted by The Game Post. "There's going to be a very intentional process for all of it that will take time."
Deane said Bungie will begin "talking about what our first step is going to look like with more clarity" at the end of October, which we're coming close to now. The Bungie boss also said the development update won't come in the form of a traditional roadmap. Instead, Bungie views it as "a progress bar" the studio hopes will "bring you all closer, more consistently to our dev milestones".
"Just be transparent about any challenges we run into and show you the proof of work along the way that unlocks further understanding," Deane explained. "That way when we share a release date we're all on the same page and have the right expectations that leads directly into how we'll further celebrate Destiny's legacy and vision for the future."
Following the 'unvaulting' Destiny 2 announcement, a Forbes report shed more light on what players can realistically expect from Bungie. The report said that removed campaigns, raids and destinations are coming back, but not expired live seasons. It also suggested that work shouldn't be taken to mean Destiny 2 is back in active development.
In June, Bungie released one final major Destiny 2 update as it announced the end of active development of the shooter-MMO. The update added much-requested features, fixed some longstanding issues and even introduced new things to play. It reignited interest in the game, seemingly enough to convince Bungie to kickstart efforts to bring back deleted content.

item.title: The developers of Umamusume: Pretty Derby have announced a sudden cancellation of an upcoming LA concert, laying the blame on an inability to receive the proper visas despite exploring "every possible option". Read more
item.description:
The developers of Umamusume: Pretty Derby have announced a sudden cancellation of an upcoming LA concert, laying the blame on an inability to receive the proper visas despite exploring "every possible option".
The concert, which was set to take place on the 22nd and 23rd October, offered digital and in-person tickets to fans of the anime horse racing franchise. These tickets are being refunded, though fans remain frustrated.
"Although we have coordinated repeatedly with all parties concerned and explored every possible option in our efforts to make this event happen, we were unable to obtain the necessary visas for entry into the US, so we have come to the painful conclusion that holding the concerts is no longer possible," the announcement message reads.
"To all the Trainers who were eagerly looking forward to the show, we sincerely apologize for the inconvenience and concern this causes, and for announcing this so close to the event date."
For fans who had planned to attend the event in-person, the announcement also notes that options are being explored to help alleviate the frustration, though nothing has been announced at this time. The cancellation announcement ends with another apology to fans, but also the Umamusume cast, company staff, and others involved in the production of the show.
Fans, as you may have guessed, are annoyed. Not at the Umamusume developers or event organisers, but rather the political realities that have led to this outcome. "I've only ever gone to one concert and I was really looking forward to vibing with everyone at the venue and making this my second. I'm not even mad, just disappointed. Cygames will never set foot in America and I don't blame them. Not after all this shit," writes X user Soramoto.
"I’d be so mad if I had to wait six months for a Visa with no response too," writes Reddit user ScorchingDragon. "Feel really bad for the people who planned a trip out to LA though. Now they have to cancel last-minute or find something else to do. At least they can go to cosplay day at Santa Anita racetrack…"
One wonders whether this situation will dissuade Cygames from organising similar events in the US in the future. Elsewhere in the video game industry, concerns surrounding US events have also continued to bubble. A number of game developers and executives expressed concerns about traveling to GDC 2026 due to changes in immigration policy.

item.description:
Origame Digital, the studio behind 2020's critically acclaimed Umurangi Generation, has just released a new game but banned it from being sold in Israel.
Penguin Colony is a Lovecraftian horror game experienced through the eyes of a penguin, based on author H.P. Lovecraft's story At the Mountains of Madness. Fellow Traveller, the game's publisher, confirmed that Penguin Colony is not on sale in Israel in a Steam community thread. The thread was created by a Steam user living in Israel wondering if the game had been delisted from Steam.
"While in general we seek to bring our games to as many potential players as possible, we believe strongly that developers have the right to control where their games are sold," Fellow Traveller replied. "In this case, the developer asked us to block sale in Israel. In the absence of more organised sanctions, this act is intended to demonstrate solidarity with Palestine. We fully support their decision."
That message is further reinforced by Penguin Colony itself, which features a post-credits scene that makes clear the studio's stance on Israel's genocide of the Palenstinan people. As shared online, the message reads: "The cowardice of the Games Industry during the ongoing genocide of Palestine by Isreal will be recorded by the art it makes."
Origame Digital has been vocal about its politics, both in and outside of its games, so this latest move is not surprising. Penguin Colony also features a strong land acknowledgement statement at its start.
"This game was made on Wurundjeri Woiwurrung land," it reads. The Kulin Nation never ceded sovereignty to the British Commonwealth. We pay respect to Elders past present and emerging as Indigenous creatives working on land that isn't our own. The land will always be Aboriginal Land no matter what."
In Penguin Colony, you play as a penguin whose home has been invaded by rival human factions searching for an ancient being. You can jump between the different penguins of the colony as you witness and attempt to evade the chaos. The game is currently available on PC, with console editions planned for 2027.
Recently, House House, the studio behind one of this year's most celebrated games, Big Walk, said the game does not have an Xbox version because parent company Microsoft is one of the BDS boycott's targets. Microsoft has ties with the state of Israel that include providing its military with cloud and AI systems used in the ongoing genocide.

item.title: Digital Sun - the indie studio behind moreish roguelike Moonlighter and moody RTS Cataclismo - has delayed a planned Steam playtest for its next game, ReVamp, citing concerns over "games being reverse-engineered, cloned and published before the original is even out." Read more
item.description:
Digital Sun - the indie studio behind moreish roguelike Moonlighter and moody RTS Cataclismo - has delayed a planned Steam playtest for its next game, ReVamp, citing concerns over "games being reverse-engineered, cloned and published before the original is even out."
The developer was planning to let folks into its vampiric "Tower Defensevania" ReVamp near the end of this spooky month, but a new trend of gen-AI copycats cloning both old and unreleased games left the studio worried.
"So many of you signed up for ReVamp's first playtest here on Steam (thank you!), but we've decided to start with something more contained on our Discord, with the public playtest coming a bit later," the developer wrote in a recent Steam blog post.
Digital Sun pointed the finger at "news of games being reverse-engineered, cloned and published before the original is even out," and worried that "sharing a build with tens of thousands of players" months prior to its full launch is "too big a risk."
From here, Digital Sun will grant access to ReVamp's first playtest in waves starting from the 29th of October, via Discord. "Even if you don't get in right away, we'd love for you to join the conversation around ReVamp as we let more players in. We hope to open the public playtest around January. To everyone who requested access here on Steam: we're sorry for the change of plans, and thank you for your patience," the studio added.
ReVamp launches in full on 25th March, 2027. Here's hoping the move can successfully shoo away any would-be clones.
Digital Sun isn't the only developer having to work around the gen-AI boom. Xbox recently announced an entire department that sounds like it's focused on gen-AI game-making, as just one example.
Meanwhile, Alliance Arts outright cancelled a Steam Next Fest demo for its anime-inspired Russian Roulette game, Drunken Goddess Reflux, because of similar issues. "We are concerned that, based on the content of the demo, works imitating or replicating this game's presentation and gameplay could be quickly produced using AI or other tools and released ahead of the game's launch," the company said last week.
Steam Next Fest 2026 should be a great occasion to discover new and exciting games that were previously nowhere near your radar. However, as we reported earlier today, the shadow of generative AI looms over the entire event and could dampen an otherwise great Steam tradition.

item.title: Final Fantasy 7 Revelation will let players access Hard Mode from the very beginning of the journey, unlike FF7 Remake and Rebirth, which made folks roll credits before unlocking the tougher difficulty option. Read more
item.description:
Final Fantasy 7 Revelation will let players access Hard Mode from the very beginning of the journey, unlike FF7 Remake and Rebirth, which made folks roll credits before unlocking the tougher difficulty option.
The tidbit comes courtesy of director Naoki Hamaguchi, who told Hardcore Gamer that Final Fantasy 7 Revelation's Hard Mode "won't function in the exact same way" as it did previously. For next year's third and final chapter, the team "reimagined the high-difficulty experience to align with the new game design."
You see, this time around, the world of Gaia supposedly opens up really early in the game. Cloud and company can fly straight to some of the game's toughest battles as soon as they jump into their flying airship, whether they're ready for the fight or not, so Square Enix's approach to difficulty had to change too.
"Hard Mode is selectable from the very start of this game," Hamaguchi explained. "Therefore, players who want to tackle challenging battles and high-difficulty gameplay right from the beginning can enjoy that experience from their very first playthrough. This is because, unlike Remake and Rebirth, Revelation offers a wide variety of end-game content even after you've beaten the game. Rather than relying solely on the traditional flow of challenging Hard Mode after beating the game, we aimed to create a game where players can enjoy various new content and challenges even after completing the main story."
As much as I loved both Remake and Rebirth, the combat never properly pushed me to my limits and tested my creaky reflexes until I finally reached that second playthrough - in the case of Rebirth, that meant playing the game for at least 50 hours. FF7 Revelation is shaping up to be another behemoth that could easily take 100 hours to fully complete, apparently, so I'm very relieved to hear that I can get to the good stuff from the jump. Hard Mode is truly where these games shine.
In a separate tweet, Hamaguchi also shared there'll be a Dynamic Mode at launch, like in Rebirth, "allowing players to enjoy consistently challenging battles throughout the game." It also looks like we'll be able to adjust how tricky those many, many mini-games are. (Damn you, Moogles!)
Final Fantasy 7 Revelation is coming to PC, PS5, Nintendo Switch 2 and Xbox Series X/S on 8th April, 2027.

item.title: Arc Raiders is still going strong almost a year after finding viral success, and it's all thanks to Embark Studios' one-two-punch strategy of launching a huge new update, Frozen Trails, to coincide with a free weekend. Read more
item.description:
Arc Raiders is still going strong almost a year after finding viral success, and it's all thanks to Embark Studios' one-two-punch strategy of launching a huge new update, Frozen Trails, to coincide with a free weekend.
Arc Raiders' Frozen Trails update upgraded the extraction shooter to version 2.0 earlier this month - 8th October - and quickly led to a surge in Steam players interested in its tense PvEvP shootouts. A new report from Alinea Analytics' Rhys Elliott now claims a similar resurgence took place across all platforms where the game's available.
According to the report, Arc Raiders' comeback peaked with a whopping 1.7m daily players jumping in on the 14th of October, its biggest player count in six months, mostly driven by the aforementioned update. What's perhaps most interesting is that player numbers actually peaked just after the game's free trial weekend ended on 12th October - though around 150,000 new looters reportedly joined the robo-infested wasteland during that weekend period.
Both events coincided with the game's steepest discount yet, slashing its price tag by 50% to $19.99. In the three days after the free trial, Arc Raiders sold another 150,000 copies and brought home roughly $3m, not counting microtransactions, per the report.
Embark Studios' seemingly went all out this month. Frozen Trails itself nudged almost every corner of the game, adding a new map, new weapons, new menacing mechs and much more.
A PvE test also tried to accommodate the game's surprisingly friendly community between the 13th and 20th of October. Executive producer Aleksander Grøndal recently said the team isn't against the idea of permanently splitting Arc Raiders' PvEvP gameplay into PvE and PvP pockets. Who knows? Doing so could open the door to another resurgence if done well.
Earlier this month, we learned the production company behind this summer's big screen horror hit, Backrooms, is working to adapt both Arc Raiders and The Finals into film and TV projects. Developer Embark is involved, too.

item.description:
Ken Kutaragi, the founder of PlayStation and architect of the first three PlayStation consoles, has said that people being upset about Sony's discontinuation of game discs is probably a "mentality issue". He understands it, he noted, but that doesn't make it "economically reasonable" for Sony to keep printing them.
Kutaragi was speaking to Video Games Chronicle at the Game Republic New Horizons event, where he said: "I understand that physical discs have become a metaphor for 'owning' games. I really understand that mentality... But nobody thinks [physical media] is necessary for a networked device like a smartphone, for example, because people feel that they will keep their content. So it's a mentality.
"I really understand [why some people are upset]," he added, "but I don't think it's economically reasonable. Maybe it's a mentality issue."
Kutaragi retired from PlayStation in June 2007, shortly after the PlayStation 3's European release, so he's been out of the company for a while. Two generations of consoles have passed since he left, though I'm sure he has close ties to Sony and people working there still. "I'm not the CEO at PlayStation any more," he noted in the interview, "but we still have some common [view points]."
Maybe Sony is pushing towards an all-digital device, he remarked, in a similar way that we see smartphones and other devices. "Maybe that's how those people are thinking," he said. "But this has caused some friction with game enthusiasts."
Kutaragi's advice? Harness AI and cloud computing to their full potential and "we won't need any console". I don't think that'll go down terribly well, Ken.

item.title: The Japan Actors Union has issued new rules, guidelines, and restrictions related to AI-generated voice use. This includes an outright ban on the replication of the voices of dead actors, unless the actor had authorised its use during their lifetime. Read more
item.description:
The Japan Actors Union has issued new rules, guidelines, and restrictions related to AI-generated voice use. This includes an outright ban on the replication of the voices of dead actors, unless the actor had authorised its use during their lifetime.
Per Automaton, these guidelines are meant to protect an industry that has been exposed to exploitation by generative AI. One example includes voice actor Kenjiro Tsuda (Jujutsu Kaisen and Chainsaw Man) taking Tiktok to court in an attempt to remove AI-generated voice imitations from the platform. He would go on to lose that case, but not without setting a precedent that a person's voice is subject to protection under publicity rights laws.
The guidelines cover four major points. The first is focused on consent and establishes that permission must be granted at "every stage" of the generative AI process. This would mean AI companies require permission from actors before models are trained on their performances.
The second point, meanwhile, states that AI replications of an actor's work are to be counted as a new performance under the guidelines. This would mean royalties or compensation must be paid by AI companies to the actors involved.
Next up comes generative AI-powered translations, which takes an actor's performance and automatically changes it to another language. These must maintain the "artistic integrity" of the original performance, the guidelines state, and may not be used without permission in overseas regions.
"The Japan Actors Union will strive to not just establish these guidelines as industry-wide rules, but also strengthen its efforts to encourage the government to legislate regulations that protect 'voice rights'," wrote The Japan Actors Union (translated by Automaton). "Technological advancements will not stop, but the 'living, breathing human expression' and a 'respect for rights' must always remain at its core."
It is worth noting that these guidelines are not laws and therefore are not binding rules AI companies must follow. Even so, it marks a major push from the Japan Actors Union for this to change. These new guidelines contribute to mounting pressure against the generative AI industry in Japan, as actors continue to push for better protections.
Japan's Voice Actor Union is not the only one pushing back against generative AI. In Western countries, similar collectives have been speaking out about the technologies' impact on the field, with one describing it as "catastrophic".

item.title: Bullet-dodging PlayStation shooter Saros has welcomed a sizeable Zenith update today, which has the twin aims of making the game both more accessible for those who haven't played it (or are struggling to get into it) and more replayable for those who have. Read more
item.description:
Bullet-dodging PlayStation shooter Saros has welcomed a sizeable Zenith update today, which has the twin aims of making the game both more accessible for those who haven't played it (or are struggling to get into it) and more replayable for those who have.
The headline additions are a quickfire boss-rush mode, a New Game Plus mode, an entire new layer of modifiers to make runs easier and harder, and - very appealingly - a slow-mo option to slow the game down.
The Slow Game Speed option can be varied depending on preference and can be activated either manually or automatically. You choose how much it slows the game down by; a video of it makes it look a lot like slow-mo in many other games, providing crucial thinking time in Saros you otherwise struggle to get.
Developer Housemarque said in a blog post it was "always wary" about toning down its games. "Although we realise our games can look intimidating at first, we didn’t want to compromise the combat system of Saros by reducing the projectiles that put the 'bullet' in 'bullet ballet'," it said. Hence the new slow game speed.
The new game modifiers allow you to tune the difficulty depending on what kind of challenge you're up for. If you want a bit of help, there are 10 new Protection modifiers you can apply. An example given was of a Corruption Melee Enhancement, which unleashes the game's deadly Corruption that builds up on you for huge melee damage.
Meanwhile, if you want to make the game harder, there are Trial modifiers. An example given was of Hostile Regeneration, which allows crowd-controlled enemies to quickly regain health unless you close to melee and finish them off with a strike.
The New Game Plus mode is called Eclipse Layers, and it activates once you've cleared the game. Each new Eclipse Layer represents a more intense version of the game with altered rules, apparently, and each has various prerequisites required in unlocking it; some require a certain amount of modifiers to be in effect, for example.
In step with this, Arjun now wears a cool sun-like crown during the Eclipse Layers - and his armour glows golden - that grows depending on the modifiers you have in play. The crown is also essential for seeing 12 new story visions Housemarque has added to the game for you to find.
Finally, Overlord Rush is the boss-rush mode that's designed to be played in 10-minute bursts, giving you a 'set' of the game's bosses to fight. A final set - Totality, it's called - has you face all eight Overlords in one continuous gauntlet.
Saros released in April on PS5 and was well reviewed, though it had a sluggish start in terms of sales, especially compared to predecessor of sorts, Returnal. Housemarque doesn't seem concerned, though, saying "this is just the start of the discussion", and that there's plenty to "tweak and add" and work will continue for "a while". This Zenith update is presumably a major part of that work.

item.description:
This year has seen two highly-rated and beloved Star Wars games in the XCOM-like Zero Company, and the Burnout-like Galactic Racer. And both were made by independent studios rather than much bigger companies, which have typically taken on Star Wars games in recent years, such as Ubisoft with Star Wars Outlaws and EA with Star Wars Battlefront.
The change, it turns out, was intentional. Lucasfilm Games bigwig Douglas Reilly told The Game Business that the Star Wars franchise stewards are now much more open about who to give the license to.
"We're obviously a licensing business," Reilly explained, "so we're not the publishers any more of products. Our goal is to try and find a publishing partner and a developer or a publisher and a developer. I think we've tried to be more flexible about who we're willing to take pitches from. Good ideas can come from a lot of different places."
This is a fairly recent change in Lucasfilm Games' strategy. The license holder was previously happy to sell a single publisher exclusive rights to Star Wars games, which previously was EA. That approach has often been criticised for limiting the creative output, be it in the number of games released or genres that get chosen. That dearth is something Star Wars fans truly felt when EA had exclusive rights to Star Wars, but this new approach allows for a much more varied pool of games and more frequent releases.
To that end, Reilly revealed there is no particular tier of publisher that Lucasfilm Games targets, saying, "There are some hurdles; we have a high quality bar and we want to make sure they're excellent experiences. And that means typically you work with more experienced teams than new teams." However, that doesn't mean you "necessarily [have to] be a top-five publisher to make a great Star Wars game".
Reilly also teased what we can expect from Star Wars games in the future. "We're exploring all kinds of things, large and small," he said, "with partners that I think are going to continue to surprise folks who are like, 'Oh, they're doing a thing with them. That might be interesting to see how that turns out.'"
The number of currently announced Star Wars games remains small. Outside of Quantic Dream's long-in-development Star Wars Eclipse, the only other game that's understood to be in the works is the third game in Respawn's Star Wars Jedi series. Former Mass Effect and Knights of the Old Republic lead Casey Hudson is currently working on a follow-up, Fate of the Old Republic, as Saber Interactive continues to insist the Knights of the Old Republic Remake remains in development.

item.description:
It took me longer than I'd like to admit to realise something obvious about Star Wars Zero Company. The fate of its eponymous crew - short of cash, betrayed by the shifting sands of circumstance in a tumultuous wider world, scrambling to just about get the job over the line - is really a lot like that of its developers at Bit Reactor. Furloughed for about a month before the game was released, those staff have clearly hustled and scrapped and fought to the last. And so Zero Company the game bears the signs of its development. In places it feels a little patched together, a little under-ready, a game that launched into the world like a roguish pilot might launch a half-repaired starfighter. The windscreen's rattling, warning lights are flashing, one particularly hirsute engineer is deeply unimpressed at the decision to take off, and nobody knows where that ominous groaning noise is coming from. But somehow she's up. And in the end that's all that counts.
Zero Company is not a tidy game, then - truly, I've a list of nitpicks longer than this review - but it is also a bit of a gem. There's so much love here. At times it borders on the saccarine, some characters getting a little too wistful, moments of crewmate dialogue a little too breathy, too aww, shucks. But I've an enduring soft spot for games where you can feel the development of it as you play. And it's more than just the slightly taped-together vibes that give Zero Company that impression here. You can feel the development of this game because you can feel the thinking behind it. The many hours that years-long experts of turn-based tactics (many Bit Reactor devs have pedigree at Firaxis, developer of the modern XCOM games) have spent sat in, I'd like to imagine, a big, comfortable chair. Perhaps with their feet resting, legs crossed, up on their desk. And staring intently at the ceiling until the solution to one design problem or another presented itself. A game I imagine as being developed much the same as it's played.
A nice twist, however, is in how relaxed that playing can be. Zero Company's default difficulty is on the easy side, pitched at newcomers to the turn-based tactical genre, and in turn it makes for a perfect match to the source material. Star Wars Zero Company is set in the late Clone Wars era - roughly parallel to Episode 3, in other words - which also happens to be the prime kids TV era. This is the time when Obi Wan Kenobi was a cool action figure warrior-general with big shoulder pads and there were lots of Trooper dudes with names like Rex diving around shooting their lasers. It's also the period that plays home to Andor, the gloriously realised political melodrama about revolution, solidarity, and the banality of evil under fascism, perched right at the opposite end of the Star Wars Seriousness Spectrum. And so Zero Company has these two, ostensibly opposing threads running through it, tasking it with somehow tying together light entertainment and timely introspection. And somehow, it does it quite well.
The default difficulty is part of the reason why (though there are hard and ironman-like modes for the true tacticos and sickos out there, of course). There's a novelty to angling a game in this genre - a genre more often associated with those iron men - at the casual crowd, in aiming for breeziness and satisfaction first. This is my first time enjoying one of these games as a good old-fashioned romp, where there might be the occasional grabbing of a hat beneath the closing door but, broadly speaking, you will find yourself playing as the good guys who ultimately always come out on top.
That pairs nicely with Zero Company's take on telling a story. Rather than the XCOM approach of an aggressively replayable campaign with a feather-light narrative layer, Zero Company has a proper beginning-middle-end story. This is where the Andor side of things comes in. Zero Company is far from that level of writing and execution, unfortunately, and perhaps expectedly. It relays its themes broadly and a little clunkily, falling into familiar video game traps that so often feel unavoidable because of the way the game itself is structured.
Characters, for instance, often need to deliver entire backstories in a couple of throwaway lines - lines which most players might never hear because they didn't opt to talk to the right static NPC between the right missions. Or which they might hear a variation of multiple times because they talked to them at every opportunity, and developers need to make sure those skip-lots-of-conversations players get their required minimum exposition to know what's going on. There's also a lot of overly-breathy voice work - Jae, who has a moderately interesting background as a kind of ore-baron nepo baby who wants to do good, is a particular culprit of the kind of over-earnestness that can jar just a little.
The truth is a lot of Star Wars media is always going to struggle to execute its themes with the sophistication we now know to be possible, post-Andor. But what helps Zero Company is that those themes are at least there, and more than that, they're both fully understood and delivered with heartfelt sincerity. There's a wonderful transition, which I'll try not to spoil, where this crew's story shifts from underdog adventure-romp (that's the third of Star Wars' three pillars accounted for: original trilogy ruffian-camp), through Clone Wars action melodrama, and out the other side into something about bigger ideas. I only wish it had gone on for a little longer after that point - you'll know it when you play it - to give that final part a bit more time to breathe.
All that said, I expect most people coming to Zero Company are coming because you can conveniently shorten it to ZCOM. This is a tactics game from tactics virtuosos, ultimately, and in the playing is where it really shows. The big twist for XCOM fans is the removal of the two-action limit. Here you get three, though rather than that simply feeling like action point creep - like before, but more! - it's another decision I can feel the armchair thinking in. The genius of two is the simplicity, and the tension that comes from it. Move and shoot, or move further? By moving to three action points - but, crucially, in doing so making some actions cost one point, some two, some three or all the points you have left - you introduce a new kind of tension. Now it matters even more which character shoots first, and at whom.
An example: Trick, a trusty ex-Republic trooper, has an automatic 'repeater' blaster that, when used, consumes all his remaining action points, doing more damage the more he has left to spend. This means he can only ever shoot at one enemy per turn, but also that he can do a lot of damage to that one enemy if he stays still. Or he can move quite far - two thirds of the maximum range - and still do a little damage at the end. Now you have an interesting choice to make: do you make Trick a single-target nuke for taking chunks of HP out of elites? Or do you send him off on quests to pick off puny, dead-in-one-shot battle droids? Over the course of a single battle he could be both.
All this is instantly more sophisticated when you add in each character's various abilities - both passive and active - and items. I opted for my delightfully customisable main character, Hawkes, to be a sharpshooter, giving him a sniper rifle and some excellent sniper-related skills. He can zero in, gaining a load of stacks of lethality - critical chance, accuracy - in exchange for one of his three points. That sniper rifle takes the remaining two to fire, and all those stacks are lost if he moves or is otherwise rudely displaced. He, like all named characters, also comes with a few unique aspects too, such as being able to give another ally an extra action point, and providing a couple passive buffs.
Those active abilities require you to spend a resource called Advantage, which builds up as you land hits on enemies through the course of an encounter, up to a maximum of 10. At harder difficulties or in tougher encounters this quickly becomes part of your planning: I want to use this ability, but am a little short of Advantage. Do I instead just do something else with that character, or do I use another character to land some hits, build up the Advantage, and go with my original plan? Then the synergies start to kick in.
Cly Kullervo, for instance, has low-cost abilities such as her hugely helpful jetpack, and an electric dart you ideally want to stack up en masse, before triggering one huge, multiplying explosion. That already works nicely with her pistol, which can be fired three times for three Advantage-building hits, but it's even better if you have another character like, say, Tel-Rea Vokoss. As a Jedi Padawan (smartly introduced as a real novice, to keep her deftly balanced), she can push and pull enemies around repeatedly and into one another - both for racking up multiple hits and, if you're clever, disposing of tougher foes in one hit for a bit of good old-fashioned lobbing off the edge of the map. By the end I often found myself using those two, plus Kabb Uppercut, built as an attention-drawing tank, for their excellent dovetailing kits.
But then Jae, for all her sins, has an extremely useful execution ability that picks off an enemy left on low health from almost anywhere on the map. You can work that in with one of Zero Company's other great additions, Assists, for some lovely chain reactions. Each turn, one of your operators gets the option to call for another operator who'll take a free shot at the next enemy the first operator attacks. More than once I found myself nodding proudly at my own late night reflection in the PC monitor, after triggering a chain of attack, assist, execution. Or better yet, you could use an ability to make an operator such as Kabb retaliate after getting a hit. So Kabb could, in theory, call for an assist, shoot an enemy that retaliates, have his ally shoot them for the assist, then get shot by them, then retaliate, then have Jae relieve them of their final chunk of HP from halfway across the map. You could use an ability that lets Kabb assist the next ally who attacks. You could build him so he does lots of extra assist damage. On and on.
The missions themselves are, broadly speaking, enjoyable enough. There are a couple of standouts - escaping along a long bridge that's being blown up behind you is good fun, as are a couple of similarly dynamic missions right towards the end of the story. A few too many follow a slightly rote format of going in and rescuing a temporary extra party member, activating a button, or standing in a zone, although these are the ones that get a fair bit more enjoyable when the challenge is higher.
These are also, typically, the more optional missions, which is where the other half of Zero Company comes in. Like so many others in the genre, there's an element of base management to be overseen between the missions themselves. This time, in what feels like a nod to another Firaxis game in Marvel's Midnight Suns, that base is a physical space you can run around in third-person. This is where those largely static NPCs loiter, your crewmates waiting to pop out a little exposition or mission-by-mission character development on request. At times they are actually quite lovely - I will forever love Kabb's strangely endearing cockney-like dialect, where he seems to speak entirely in rhymey-timey versions of the types of idioms I have spent my life aggressively editing out of video game reviews.
Specific places in your base also act as the various necessary upgrade stations. Each character has a skill tree - later upgraded into two skill trees, the second offering a choice of any character class, which is a nice twist. These are a relatively light touch, some upgrades doing the classic plus-some-percent-crit-chance that can slide under the radar somewhat. But many, even with minor improvements, have a subtly important impact. Upgrading a skill all the way to the end of the tree just to take it from two Advantage points cost to one sounds minor, but can make all the difference in a tight encounter. And those crit chances can, at least, be built up to really significant levels, where with the right play there's a good chance of a crit on almost every shot taken.
Slightly less effective are the Black Market store and the upgrades to the base itself. Both of these were, in my experience, just too expensive to actually implement to the point of making a meaningful difference. On standard difficulty I bought maybe one item in my entire run, the rest being earned as rewards or from various other upgrades (all of this with in-universe credits earned from completing missions, to be clear). Likewise with the base upgrades: the rewards from missions mean you can afford to take roughly one upgrade per 'cycle', with each upgrade typically taking one or two cycles to complete, and you later being able to do two or three upgrades at a time. All of which is to say: you just upgrade them one at a time, with little meaningful choice or strategy to the approach because you simply can't afford to do anything else.
There's a similarly light touch to Operations, a kind of mini-mission system that you must go through each cycle before you undertake that cycle's one mission. These are FTL-like choice-based, text-only scenarios - sometimes dilemmas, sometimes a choice of three equally okay rewards - that can also occasionally impact your bond with crewmates. In being text-only and largely very short and simple, they felt a smidge underrealised, almost as though the third-person view, only used around the base and in introductory snippets of main story missions, originally existed as the vehicle through which you'd be doing these operations instead, only to be cut back at some point along the way.
Bit Reactor could also have skipped the third-person sections of missions themselves. These are brief interludes or prologues to the main story missions themselves, and often little more than a case of jogging in a straight line and scanning two things when prompted. They feel like a legacy of a game with a bit more ambition than it could afford. Perhaps with another six months in the oven - with its staff having not been furloughed before the game even arrived - they'd have been cut, smartly papered over and worked around; us players never knowing they'd even existed. This is what I mean by Zero Company being a game that seems to wear its development in the open.
Lastly on the limitations front, those inter-character bonds, too, feel a little too easy to ignore. Increasing your bond with a character - by taking them on missions, doing assists with them, making Operations decisions they agree with - gives a kind of XP boost to your bond. After enough XP your Bond levels up, then you get a choice of three bonuses for both characters. The motivation then is to increase the bond through the thresholds but, as far as I could gather, that's about the only benefit, and so in the end they feel like a kind of background bonus to simply playing the game over time, rather than with any specific intentionality behind it.
These systems do, though, provide a kind of colour and texture to Zero Company that still has merit in its own right. They're layers. Most of them, on their own, can feel a little lightweight, but combined they still mesh together nicely. What Zero Company does so well is to always give you a decision to make, always a pathway to optimise, an option to prioritise. These management layers work so well over turn-based tactics games because fundamentally they're tapping into that same part of the brain: how can I best allocate my very limited resources with all the information at hand? What are tactics, after all, if not a test of maximising efficiency in a series of individual moments; a part of a strategy that tests your ability to then find that efficiency consistently over time?
This is the magic with Zero Company, ultimately. There are brilliant revisions to the formula here that add nuance and tension and decision points, layering on complexity without complication. There are wonderful moments of theming and tone: through one of Star Wars' richest moments in time, through some deeply likeable characters, and through the old chestnut of emergent storytelling too, as you scramble to get your no-name Glupp Shitto-alike out of one particularly hairy mission alive. And there's depth here if you wish to mine for it. But above all it's just another example of an endlessly winning formula. Of action figures, cartoons, dramas, chessboards, and bottomless pits you can drop bad guys into, with all the glorious, goofball sounds and sights that Star Wars can slather over the top. And on top of all that, it's a game with its developers' earnest effort bursting through it at every opportunity. It's not perfect. It's also just impossible not to love.
A copy of Star Wars Zero Company was provided for this review by EA.

item.title: CD Projekt Red is currently rolling the promised Switch 2 patch for The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt - Remastered, addressing a number of issues in the game. Read more

CD Projekt Red is currently rolling the promised Switch 2 patch for The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt - Remastered, addressing a number of issues in the game.

The Witcher 3 Remastered update overhauls the 11-year-old role-playing game, visually modernising it as well as adding new animations and tweaking some gameplay systems, including skills and enemy behaviour.
